]]>Dan Dennison<![CDATA[Social welfare, tax changes and childcare costs: Everything we know about Budget 2027 so far]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/09/16/budget-2027-heres-what-we-know-so-far/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/09/16/budget-2027-heres-what-we-know-so-far/Mon, 05 Oct 2026 16:01:49 +0000Budget 2027, to be presented on October 6th, is due to involve a package of €8.5 billion, with €7 billion in additional spending and €1.5 billion in tax reductions. The cost-of-living issue will be a key focus across the whole package.

Spending – the main issues

While the €7 billion figure is large, an increase of about 6 per cent on this year, much of this money is already effectively allocated to various budgets to keep pace with inflation.

There will, however, be key decisions to be made in areas such as health – which is already running well above budget for this year – and education and in what to allocate for a new public sector pay deal. And, of course, in welfare, one of the mainstays of any budget package.

Tax – the main issues

The €1.5 billion package leaves limited enough room for manoeuvre.

Budget 2027: ‘Specific consideration’ for measures to tackle rising heating oil costs

If the bulk of the money were directed to income tax cuts it would allow the system to be adjusted for inflation and higher wages but not much more than that.

Minister for Finance Simon Harris has suggested that some money could be raised in tax increases to help pay for bigger reductions – a packet of cigarettes is set to move to €20, though extra tax revenue here will be limited. The bank levy, raising €200 million, is expected to be renewed for another year.

But Ministers will also have to find money to make some adjustment on inheritance tax and on some new business measures. And to pay the full year cost of the 9 per cent VAT rate for hospitality, announced last year.

Social protection

How much will be allocated to social protection – or welfare – will be a key issue. After some coming and going a general increase of €10 a week has been decided on, the same as the last budget.

The main welfare rates and pensions will be increased by this amount, though the main child benefit rate may stay where it is.

Promises to address child poverty are likely to see additional payments for people on welfare with children – known as child support payments – and possibly also expansions of the Working Family Payment, which is paid to lower-income families on lower earnings.

The much-discussed second tier of child benefit payments which would be paid to all lower income families is not, however, expected to happen this year.

Eligibility for the carers’ allowance is due to be extended, allowing people who have somewhat higher incomes to qualify.

Energy package

All things energy are hugely politically sensitive and will be central to the package. There will be three key elements – the carbon tax, excise taxes and cash supports to households.

A key focus will be additional supports for those struggling with energy bills through channels such as the fuel allowance scheme or household benefits packages, which help lower-income families meet daily bills.

So far the Government has resisted the return of energy credits – once-off cash payments to households to lower bills – saying it favoured more targeted, permanent measures. However, with energy prices remaining high, they have not been completely ruled out yet.

A big issue will be excise taxes on fuel. These were reduced in two steps earlier this year and the first step to the return of normal rates had been due to take place in November. Harris indicated in the Dáil on September 24th that the Coalition will push the date when this will happen through the winter.

A Government taskforce has been looking at the area of permanent supports to help households deal with energy costs. As part of this, the budget is likely to have something to say on supports for encouraging retrofitting in older homes and there will also be a scrappage scheme for old boilers, which has already been announced. Grants of €600 are also coming for those installing storage batteries as part of a solar panels investment. This is in addition to grants of up to €1,800 already available for solar PV installations.

The fuel allowances, paid to 470,000 households during the colder months, looks set to increase by €5 a week to €43.

Annual carbon tax increases had been due to be given the go-ahead, as part of a planned series of increases up to 2030. But a big shake-up here is likely.

The Coalition has indicated that there will be measures to actually reduce the price of home heating oil. The expected route would be to reduce the existing rate of carbon tax on the fuel. The Coalition could also rule out further carbon tax increases on home heating oil and gas for the rest of its term.

Delaying planned carbon tax increases or reducing existing ones raises questions for spending, as revenue from this tax pays for areas such as SSIA grants for retrofitting – which the Government is trying to speed up – certain fuel-related welfare supports and some climate friendly programmes for farmers..

Disability supports

The Programme for Government commits to a permanent cost-of-disability payment to reflect the higher costs disabled people face in their daily lives. Minister for Social Protection Dara Calleary had a public consultation on it earlier this year.

A move looks on the cards in the budget, but it appears likely that it will be less than campaigners are looking for. Social Justice Ireland has said a €20-a-week payment would cost €242 million in a year.

A new disability support payment will be announced, but on a lesser scale, involving one or two lump sum payments a year. It looks likely to be €500 a year.

Income tax

An increase in the level at which the higher 40 per cent income tax rate kicks in looks certain. The current rate is €44,000 for a single person and €53,000 for a married couple.

An increase of €2,000 had been speculated. That would be worth €400 a year to someone who earns enough to get the full benefit. However, Harris may have the firepower to go a bit further.

Harris will also indicate that the Government intends to increase the level at which the higher tax rate applies in successive budgets for the rest of its term.

For this budget, as many lower earners would gain nothing from an increase in the level at which the higher rate kicks in, there are also likely to be significant increases in tax credits. These would benefit all income tax payers, but give the highest proportional gain to the lower earners.

The budget will confirm the Government’s decision on an increase in the minimum wage. The Low Pay Commission recommended increasing it by 79 cent per hour, bringing the adult rate from €14.15 to €14.94 per hour from next January and it appears this will be accepted.

There will be a tweak in the entry level for the 3 per cent USC rate to make sure no one on the new minimum wage pays at this level.

Income tax change is coming in Budget 2027. Here’s what it means for you

People who get up early were left disappointed by Varadkar. Harris is ready to try again

Tax and Housing

First time buyers will be able to access up to €35,000 towards the deposit on their first home, under the Help-to-Buy scheme, after agreement was reached by party leaders. This increases the limit by €5,000.

There also looks set to be an increase in the rent tax credit, which is worth up to €1,000 per year to a single renter and €2,000 to a couple.

With interest rates on the up, there will be a focus on whether the mortgage tax credit will be renewed. This year it was worth 50 per cent of the increase in mortgage interest paid in 2026 versus 2022, capped at a maximum tax credit of €625.

Martin has hinted that there might also be an improvement in the rent-a-room tax allowances, which allows homeowners to earn up to €14,000 a year from renting out a room to a long-term renter (staying for at least 28 days). The suggestion is that this might rise by €2,000 - a higher increase had been mooted earlier. There may be conditions attached.

Inheritance tax

There have been hints from all sides of Government that there would be some move here. Pre-budget documents drawn up by civil servants warned of the high cost of fundamental reform of the tax, such as aligning the tax relief for wider groups inheriting to the levels which currently apply to children.

So it appears there will be modest increases in the three thresholds. The Category A threshold of €400,000 is paid by children inheriting from parents. The Category B threshold of €40,000 applies – generally – to siblings, nieces, nephews, grandchildren and grandparents who get inheritances. The Category C threshold of €20,000, applies in most other cases.

Capital Gains Tax

Senior Ministers have also referred to the possibility of capital gains tax moves, and Harris has said that the 33 per cent rate is “objectively too high”. There may be some limited move to reduce it.

There could be an extension of some CGT reliefs, such as those available to entrepreneurs and a commitment to look at the whole capital tax system, particularly as it relates to investment. The rate of the so-called deemed disposal tax, which put a charge on profits from investments in exchange traded funds every eight years, looks set to be cut from 38 per cent to 35 per cent.

Savings Scheme

The Minister for Finance is due to announce key details of his savings scheme. The outline shape has already been revealed – it will offer tax-free investment options for households in stocks and shares subject to certain limits. The key question is what these will be. The budget is due to reveal three key things.

The first is a limit capping what individuals can put in each year. The second is the total level of a savings fund that will remain free of all taxes. The third is the level of a new special tax rate that will apply to the assets in the fund above this limit – which may be 1 per cent, according to reports.

Childcare

As part of its cost-of-living package, the Government has promised further help for parents. Its programme promises to cap monthly costs at €200 per child, with progress made over the term of the Coalition. Higher investment to providers under the so-called core funding scheme was already announced to apply from September2026, together with weekly fee caps for parents.

This budget is set to announce a headline reduction of some €1,000 a year for parents of children in full-time care ( 45 hours a week) up to senior infants age. This will be achieved through an increased subsidy under the National Childcare Scheme - paid to providers and deducted from bills - and a cut in the cap on fees. Exact details are due to be finalised on Monday. Earlier reports had suggested this could come into effect in January, though the suggestion now is next September. There will also be measures to support the earnings of people working in the sector.

Harris has also hinted at increased tax relief for those minding a child or children in their home. At the moment a minder can earn up to €15,000 tax free per year for minding a maximum of three children – not counting their own.

Third level

It is expected that there will be an across-the-board €150 cut to student fees. A proposal to cut student fees by €250 a year was reportedly under discussion in late negotiations, but hopes for this had expired by Monday morning. Across the course of the day, however, the idea re-emerged, albeit at a lesser amount, with indications on Monday evening that there would be an extra allocation of around €18 million to deliver the measure.

Some relief appears to be on the cards for families who have more than one child in college through an extension of current discounts which apply to some families.

Culture Giveaway

A plan had emerged to give a €100 voucher 16 year-olds in the Budget to be used for attending arts, music or culture events. A proposal to give such a voucher to 16 and 17 year-olds was part of the Programme for Government. It had appeared that this was going to be subject to further study, but the latest reports say the card will feature in some form in the budget speech.

Business

The Government has made general promises on supporting businesses, but what could happen remains unclear. An extension of research and development relief could be one potential avenue, as well as measures aimed at encouraging investment in domestic industry.

Businesses are also looking for higher spending on training, funded by a surplus in the National Training Fund, but it is not clear is this will happen. It appears now that this is on the cards, with an allocation from the fund for training in AI related areas. A sum of €150 million over three years may be involved.

The slowdown in price growth has been linked to expectations of higher borrowing costs with the European Central Bank (ECB) in the process of raising interest rates and comes amid the uncertain geopolitical outlook.

A global bond market sell-off is also pushing up borrowing costs in many countries.

In the euro area, loans with an initial fixed-rate period of 10 years-plus rose by 8 basis points to 3.43 per cent in August and the surge in euro zone government yields in recent weeks is expected to push rates even higher.

]]><![CDATA[Female-looking AI agents were paid less than male ones in virtual office, study finds]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/2026/10/05/female-looking-ai-agents-were-paid-less-than-male-ones-in-virtual-office-study-finds/https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/2026/10/05/female-looking-ai-agents-were-paid-less-than-male-ones-in-virtual-office-study-finds/Mon, 05 Oct 2026 11:19:34 +0000Gender bias in the workplace can be replicated in interactions with artificial intelligence, new research from the University of Limerick (UL) has found.

The study examined whether the way AI assistants are presented influences how people treat them in a workplace setting.

It was co-authored by Dr Mary Hausfeld of UL’s Kemmy Business School.

Researchers placed 189 workers in a virtual reality office and asked them to complete work-related tasks with different AI assistants, including human-like agents presented with either male or female appearance.

Participants were then given real money to divide between themselves and the AI assistant for completing the tasks, allowing the researchers to “recreate a real-world transaction and examine how much people were willing to pay AI for its work”.

AI agents with a female appearance were paid less than their male-presenting counterparts, despite using the same underlying technology, according to the research.

The AI agents had the same underlying capabilities, yet participants treated them differently depending on how they were presented.

The male-presenting AI agent, Johan, received higher monetary rewards than the female-presenting agent, Johanna. The male agent was also perceived as more human-like.

Johanna was paid 10.25 per cent less than Johan for completing the same work.

The researchers concluded that their findings suggest gender biases familiar from human workplaces could be reproduced in interactions with AI.

Hausfeld said the results raise important questions as AI agents increasingly become part of people’s working lives.

“What is striking about our findings is that the technology behind these AI agents was exactly the same, but people did not treat them in the same way.

“We often think of AI as being neutral, but the way we design and present these systems can activate those same assumptions and biases that exist in our interactions with other people.

“As AI agents become more common in the workplace, we need to think carefully about the characteristics we give them and the behaviours those choices may encourage. We don’t want to inadvertently reproduce existing inequalities in a new technological setting.”

The study was part of a larger investigation into how the human-like appearance of AI influences workplace interactions.

Although the systems were powered by the same underlying AI, participants trusted the human-like assistants more and gave them more credit for their contribution than the robot.

Participants also suggested they had no preference for an AI with female or male attributes, but “their behaviour told a different story”.

The study was conducted by Isabelle Cuber and Tarek Alakmeh of the University of Zurich, Mary Hausfeld of University of Limerick, Anand van Zelderen of SKEMA Business School, and Moritz Jenny, Jochen Menges and Thomas Fritz of the University of Zurich.

Human-Like and Male? How AI Assistant Design Relates to Trust and Monetary Reward at Work in VR will be presented at the 14th Nordic Conference on Human-Computer Interaction in Vaasa, Finland, from October 5th to 7th.

It will also be published in the conference proceedings by the Association for Computing Machinery.

During budget week last October, Minister for Culture and Media Patrick O’Donovan said he would like to revisit the regional uplift despite its exclusion from the tax package. However, the Coalition did unveil a separate enhancement to the section 481 specifically aimed at the State’s growing visual effects industry.

]]><![CDATA[Should I start a message with ‘I hope you’re well’? If not well, should I say so?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/opinion/2026/10/05/joe-humphreys-please-dont-tell-me-you-hope-i-am-well-because-i-might-just-answer/https://www.irishtimes.com/opinion/2026/10/05/joe-humphreys-please-dont-tell-me-you-hope-i-am-well-because-i-might-just-answer/Mon, 05 Oct 2026 05:00:00 +0000Dear reader, I hope you are well. Let me get that out of the way, because I won’t be saying it again.

I’m fed up with the “I hope you are well” trend in emails, WhatsApps and other communications.

The use of the phrase really took off during the Covid-19 pandemic, according to business observers – an understandable urge given the deadly virus then circulating. But today we just have the usual hazards that come with being human. So what’s wrong with a simple “hello”?

I’m not against inquiring into another person’s welfare, but “I hope you are well” has become too reflexive, too automatic for my tastes. Literally, it’s on auto-prompt. Starting typing “I hope ... ” and then swipe right to complete the rest.

Responding meaningfully to “hope you’re well” has become another task to tick off. And when the phrase is in corporate communications, it seems cloying or indecently chummy.

A more honest greeting might read: “The world’s gone to shit, and no one really knows why we’re here, but have you got that report I was looking for yesterday ...”

Obviously, I do hope you are well, but can’t we take that for granted? I mean, I’m not a psychopath. Also, call me naive, but I generally assume people don’t wish me to be unwell. So, like, thanks for the concern, but suppose I’m in the depths of existential dejection; are you really ready for me to offload my feelings on you?

What does an expert think? Dr Emma Farrell is an assistant professor in mental health in the department of psychology at Maynooth University. She offers another view as today’s Unthinkable guest.

The phrase ‘hope you’re well’ can feel robotic. Should we scrap it?

“No. I can hope someone is doing well without necessarily having a close relationship with them. Indeed, the Buddhist loving-kindness meditation invites us to wish others well as a practice that connects us to our shared humanity. So while your email reflex may not have the wellbeing of humanity at its heart, it’s not likely to do any harm.”

But can someone establish how you are without being present?

“It’s very hard to establish how somebody is without direct information from the person themselves. If we see someone in person, particularly someone we know, we can often tell how they are by reading their body language, facial expressions and general energy and demeanour. I’m struck by the philosopher and sociologist Hartmut Rosa’s account of resonance: the experience of being reached by something in another person – a shadow of pain, despair or joy on their face – and responding in a way that changes the encounter. I’m not sure that kind of resonance is possible without presence.

“Without presence, we are relying much more on what people say in response to ‘I hope you’re well’. As with many social courtesies, the answer may be as reflexive as the greeting – ‘I’m great thanks, I hope you’re well too’. There’s nothing wrong with that, but we all need some people in our lives with whom we can answer that question honestly.”

What exactly is a resonant relationship, and can you create it online?

“A resonant relationship is one in which we feel that the other person reaches us, that we are safe and welcome to respond as ourselves, and that something in us shifts or is moved through the encounter. This can happen online. For someone who finds it difficult to meet people or connect in person, an online encounter may even offer a much-needed opportunity to meet someone who understands their experience.

“But I don’t think resonance comes from using the right greeting or platform or playing the ‘communication’ game well. It relies on an openness and willingness to be present to how someone actually is, what they say, what they express, or what they struggle to convey ...

“Resonance calls for space, time, attention and an openness to being affected by the other person. This openness can be hard to summon when we’re distracted, exhausted or caught up in our own worries and concerns.”

How do you create meaningful connections in a remote working context?

“There’s no special toolkit for building a connection through a screen. The same things matter in remote working contexts as physical working contexts – doing good work, being kind and showing, over time, that you’re a decent person to work with.”

Okay, I’m softening a bit on ‘hope you’re well’. Perhaps what’s really triggering me is the volume of communications online rather than one particular pleasantry per se. But why is this greeting so ubiquitous?

“The words we use to greet one another reflect the conventions of our culture and the moment we’re living in. In Ireland in 2026, ‘I hope you’re well’ is an acceptable way of saying ‘I recognise there is another human being on the other end of this exchange who has a life and needs and feelings that are worth acknowledging’ before getting down to business. Perhaps what we feel compelled to do is greet one another, rather than assess the wellbeing of everyone on our organisation’s mailing list. And that’s no bad thing.”

]]><![CDATA[Replacing beef farming with forestry would boost incomes and help meet climate goals]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/05/replacing-beef-farming-with-forestry-would-boost-incomes-and-help-meet-climate-goals/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/05/replacing-beef-farming-with-forestry-would-boost-incomes-and-help-meet-climate-goals/Mon, 05 Oct 2026 04:25:00 +0000In the early years after Independence, virtually no afforestation was undertaken in Ireland. Public funds were in scarce supply and subsistence farming was still prevalent in much of the country, and that pattern more or less continued for the next two decades because, as one government minister stated some time later, putting trees in the ground would not put more food on the table.

Years after the second World War, it dawned on the Government how dwindled timber stocks and forests had become, and despite considerable pressure being exerted within government not to support afforestation, a defined forest policy was established and actively promoted. However, as before, only poorer quality land could be afforded for planting. Until the mid-’80s, afforestation progressed, occasionally reaching an additional 9,000 hectares annually, and it was undertaken almost exclusively by the State.

Even as public afforestation was gaining a foothold, private planting was minimal, having a negative image and receiving little or no State support.

Then in the mid-’80s forestry was identified as having the potential to make a major contribution to national economic and regional development and rural incomes, and generous grants and annual premiums were provided by the State and EU.

Subsequently, afforestation trebled between 1987 and 1995, with private planting exceeding public planting for the first time in 1989.

Planting held up reasonably well in the decade after 1995, at an average of 13,000 hectares each year, but levels of planting have largely gone downhill ever since. In the past decade, new planting has averaged 3,800 hectares annually.

Afforestation in 2023 and 2024 was at its lowest level since the 1920s. Over the past 40 years a succession of ambitious planting targets were established, but all were missed by a wide margin.

The surge in private planting from the late ’80s would initially have occurred on the least intensively farmed land. Thereafter, it would have moved on to progressively better land. That would partially explain the very high planting early on.

While there are possibly many reasons for the general downward trend in planting since the mid-’90s, it began with the changed character of the EU’s Common Agricultural Policy (Cap).

Cap shifted from price and market supports to restrictive measures on output, strengthening rural development and environmental policies and direct payments.

Does Ireland have the will to undo the disaster of plantation forestry?

The pattern of land use is now facing substantial pushback due to environmental pressures, and in consequence we have reached if not surpassed peak intensity in grassland utilisation. From here, there will be increased pressure on land use due to enterprises such as anaerobic digestion, while sectors such as solar panels and onshore wind turbines are also likely to show significant development.

The Cap Strategic Plan 2023-2027 also includes two heavily funded environmental measures heralding a new era addressing biodiversity, environmental issues, water quality and climate objectives, and increasingly offering rewards for alternative land uses that were not hitherto available. These schemes have attracted a high rate of participation from farmers and pose a real challenge for forestry.

Afforestation is the most significant climate change mitigation option that is available to Ireland’s land use sector, and is an essential and recognised factor to reaching net zero carbon dioxide emissions by 2050.

The rate of afforestation depends not only on the incentives available but also on such factors as awareness levels, promotion activities and technical support systems

So, from a future perspective, any increase in forestry planting is most likely to come from the cohort of 80,000 or so beef cattle enterprises. The great majority of those involved have the lowest incomes, are older than average, at least half of them have off-farm jobs and they have lesser levels of contact with support services.

The replacement of beef farming with forestry is a win-win action. It increases farm income, reduces GHG emissions, and significantly increases carbon sequestration. There also tends to be a prevalent negative attitude to forestry from this group, ranging from perceptions that forestry is inimical to agricultural development, to it being responsible for rural depopulation, social isolation and the limiting of land-use options.

Consideration must now focus on the shape of and ambition for the next Irish afforestation programme. It is now Government policy to expand forest cover from the current 11 per cent or so of the land area of the country to 18 per cent, but based on achievements over recent decades we will be waiting a long time to reach this target.

‘Our purpose is to manage the State’s forests on behalf of the people of Ireland’

The rate of afforestation depends not only on the incentives available but also on such factors as awareness levels, promotion activities and technical support systems. At a policy level, it is necessary to adopt an integrated approach in designing land-use schemes including forestry so as to achieve compatibility and complementability between the respective measures in the next national Rural Development Programme.

The role of forestry needs to be more strongly promoted across Government, and the sector’s role in adjusting to climate change and in terms of rural development given greater emphasis. The development of knowledge transfer groups representative of the relevant stakeholders or perhaps some form of European Innovation Partnerships could play a useful role in changing attitudes towards forestry. Meanwhile, every effort must be made to reach out to those particular landholders who are the most likely target category for forestry but who are the least likely to have contact with farm support services.

Finally, it could be an opportune time to establish a national forum of the respective interests such as existed in the mid-’90s, to identify the factors impeding more rapid adoption of farm forestry and how these might be addressed.

Brendan Kearney, an economic consultant, was formerly assistant director of An Foras Talúntais, now Teagasc

]]><![CDATA[Rising debt burden poses threat to economic growth ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/10/05/rising-debt-burden-poses-threat-to-economic-growth/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/10/05/rising-debt-burden-poses-threat-to-economic-growth/Mon, 05 Oct 2026 04:00:00 +0000Ireland has had a lot of experience of public debt crises. But right now, our main problem is poor management of the exchequer’s abundant, though vulnerable, resources. This compares with other major economies, where the scale and growth of public debt looms large and is a major challenge for governments.

In the UK, France and the US, government debt exceeds 100 per cent of national income. The sustainability of their public finances is posing major political challenges.

We will see this month how the UK government proposes to square the circle of political ambition and fiscal prudence. In France, the absence of a government majority in parliament may prevent any resolution, at least until after next year’s presidential election. As for the US, thus far it is ignoring the problem, as its fiscal situation deteriorates.

We know from Ireland’s debt crises in the 1980s, and again from 2008 to 2013, that once the debt burden exceeds 100 per cent of national income, there can be no resolution without serious pain.

By 1987, our debt interest payments were absorbing 10 per cent of national income, and 20 per cent of all government expenditure. The rapid growth in these outlays over the 1980s squeezed resources for government services, and also necessitated extremely high taxes. Together that made a recipe for national misery.

Reversing the rise in indebtedness proved very painful, and took most of that decade.

Although Ireland’s national debt in the wake of the 2008 financial crash peaked at more than 160 per cent of national income, higher than in the 1980s, the burden of debt proved much more manageable.

This was due to the assistance of the bailout, and a much lower external interest rate environment in its aftermath. While the necessary austerity was very painful, it only lasted four years, not a decade. Debt interest payments peaked in 2012 at less than 6 per cent of national income, and nearly 10 per cent of government expenditure.

With a rapid economic recovery, and low interest rates internationally, our indebtedness fell dramatically. Today, government interest payments account for only 2 per cent of Ireland’s national income, and almost half of that cost is covered by interest income from the Government’s investments.

Ripping the plaster off slowly in the 1980s was more painful. A lesson from the Irish experience over both debt crises is that the faster action is taken, the less damage there will be to the economy and society. The EU and IMF, which lent us large sums, also pressed for faster action in the more recent debt crisis.

Right now, the external environment has turned nasty for governments needing to borrow. Interest rates have been driven up by the huge scale of financing needed by governments, especially the US, alongside giant borrowings to fund the AI investment splurge, and by rising inflation linked to oil and gas.

Grafton chief bets on ‘PIIGS’ boom as northern European markets stall

Interest rates could well climb further if major economies cannot bring their public finances under control and if the energy crisis is not resolved.

However, interest rates in Ireland, Portugal, Spain and Greece have risen more modestly over the last three years than in countries with major fiscal problems such as France and the UK. We the “PIIGS” [Portugal, Italy, Ireland, Greece and Spain] dealt with our debt problems a decade ago. Today, Ireland can borrow at rates very close to those of Germany, reflecting a very similar levels of indebtedness.

The US is particularly exposed, because much more of their debt is short-term, unlike most European countries, which will only need to refinance 20-30 per cent of their national debt in the coming five years

Between now and 2030, we will have to refinance 30 per cent of our national debt at today’s higher interest rates. While this will mean some rise in interest payments, the change won’t be very significant. Moreover, some of the extra cost should be offset by a higher return on government financial investments.

For the UK (whose interest bill is already 3.4 per cent of national income) and for the US (paying interest amounting to 4.8 per cent of national income), the cost of refinancing at today’s higher interest rates will add to their budgetary problems.

Greece is Ireland. Ireland is Greece

The US is particularly exposed, because much more of their debt is short-term, unlike most European countries, which will only need to refinance 20-30 per cent of their national debt in the coming five years. The high interest rates needed to dampen US inflation will hit their public finances hard.

The US president has floated a $5,000 cash inducement for all if the Republicans win the midterms. Meanwhile, in the real world, higher debt payments will squeeze resources in the UK and France for social services, health and defence, unless taxes are raised.

If public debt continues to climb, interest rates will again ratchet up. That will slow down growth in the private sector, limiting any growth dividend to spend on public services, and stifle the housing market.

Ireland’s Minister for Finance has it far luckier than his international peers.

.

]]>wildpixel<![CDATA[Fund manager charges are taking a chunk out of my retirement fund]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/04/fund-manager-charges-are-taking-a-chunk-out-of-my-retirement-fund/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/04/fund-manager-charges-are-taking-a-chunk-out-of-my-retirement-fund/Sun, 04 Oct 2026 09:00:44 +0000I’m approaching retirement and, as my pension fund has grown quite well over the years, I’m interested in taking out an approved retirement fund (ARF).

I have a query about the charges involved. A fund value of €1 million would give a pension of €40,000 a year, but you can expect to pay 1 per cent of the fund value or an additional €10,000 a year in charges.

As these charges will continue to be taken as you’re drawing your pension, they could realistically amount to hundreds of thousands of euro in total.

My pension fund has done well partly because I’ve kept costs to a minimum. So, I want an ARF with:

  • Exchange-traded funds (ETFs) from the major providers. There is a huge range of these, and typical annual costs are approx 0.1 per cent or lower.
  • Execution-only. I will buy investment advice at specific times I feel I need it, rather than paying for it on an ongoing basis as part of a bundled offering.

ARF providers, however, all seem to charge a percentage of the fund value. It doesn’t make sense that drawing a pension from a €1 million fund should cost you 10 times more in charges than a pension from a €100,000 fund.

Do you know of an ARF provider with flat-rate charges, and can you recommend anything else I should be doing to minimise these charges?

KB

Approved retirement funds (ARFs) are one way a person can take their pension on retirement.

Your pension funds will have built up over your working life either in a pensions scheme attached to your workplace where you can be one of many members or small personal schemes. When it comes to retirement you have some choices about what happens those funds.

First, you can take a certain amount of your fund tax-free. That is generally a quarter of your fund up to a maximum of €200,000. If a quarter of your fund amounts to more than this, you will pay just the standard 20 per cent rate of income tax on anything between €200,000 and €500,000.

Some people, including those employed in the public service before a certain date, are entitled to take one and a half times their salary instead.

Thereafter, there are generally two ways of drawing down your income in retirement – an annuity or an ARF.

With an annuity, you hand your fund over to an insurance company in return for an agreed annual income for life. Generally an annuity will die with the owner unless they have made provision for a survivor’s payment to a spouse from the fund.

You can choose certain features – payment of a reduced pension to a surviving spouse, minimum term of payment so the fund pays out for a set minimum number of years even if you die earlier and a provision to allow for inflation, for instance. Each of these comes at a cost, reducing the amount you receive initially.

How much you receive will also be gauged by how much you have in your fund and your general health. Smokers and the less healthy, ironically, can get a higher payment as they are not likely to be needing the fund as long as someone who can reasonably expect to live close to 20 years in retirement.

ARFs were introduced widely in 1999 and have proved popular for several reasons, not least that the rates offered under annuities became less attractive.

They allow your pension to stay invested so that it can (hopefully) grow further and, among other things, they do not die with the holder. They can be left to a spouse, a child or children, or to some other beneficiary.

Each of those scenarios has different tax treatments that we will not go into here.

You clearly know all this but it is worth explaining in some bare detail as pensions have an awful habit of confusing most people out there.

Importantly in the context of your question, there are rules in place on the minimum you must draw down from your ARF each year – a percentage figure that changes with age and can also change with the sum in the fund.

Under the age of 70, you must draw down 4 per cent of the value of your fund each year (you will be taxed by Revenue as though you have even if you draw down less) – hence your €40,000 income from a €1 million fund.

Over 70, that drawdown rises to 5 per cent. And if your fund is over €2 million in value, you need to take 6 per cent each year.

The tax you pay is determined by your income from the fund – as it is for other citizens – but, with an ARF, the responsibility for deducting that tax falls to your qualified fund manager. This is the person you have an issue with.

Under the legislation, your ARF must be managed by this qualified fund manager and they are also responsible for the paperwork involved in setting up your ARF. Under section 784A of the Taxes Consolidation Act 1997, this qualified fund manager can be a stockbroker, a life company, credit union or bank.

Critically, you are also looking for ongoing growth in your fund and they are responsible for managing that. You are not just paying a fund manager to cover the costs of paying your pension monthly; you’re paying them to grow or maintain the value of the fund.

There is no provision for bypassing this fund manager so you are stuck with them. You cannot manage the fund personally.

And you are right. Income in retirement is limited and your capacity for future earnings is diminished, so it stands to reason that you would query or challenge significant costs.

As you say, a 1 per cent fund management charge translates as €10,000 lost from your fund if the fund is around €1 million in size. For most people, with more modest funds, the charge will amount to something in the single figure thousands – €1,000 a year on a fund valued at €100,000 for instance.

To put it in context, if you are in your sixties and your fund is less than €2 million in size, this charge is equal to a quarter of the income you are expected to live on for the year from the fund.

It increases the return you need to make on your remaining investments if the fund is not to be at risk of running out of cash before you die.

You are correct that 1 per cent seems to be the “average” fund management fee – although I have also come across significantly larger figures – but that is not to say that you cannot do better.

In general, the larger the fund, the more leverage you will have to negotiate down the percentage fund management charge. Certainly, with a fund of €1 million, you should be able to find a fund manager who will oversee the fund for a percentage charge closer to 0.5 per cent or 0.4 per cent.

Royal London, for instance, says it offers funds with charges ranging from 0.4 per cent to 0.9 per cent whereas someone like Zurich opts for a flat 1 per cent rate. What you get for each of these you would need to check for yourself.

I am not permitted under Central Bank rules to recommend any specific product as I am not a registered qualified financial adviser, just a journalist.

Of course, apart from the size of your fund, the charge will be determined by the type of investment you are considering. Those looking for very active management of their fund can expect to pay a higher charge all other things being equal. Clearly, investing in ETFs, which have low costs, should be at the lower end of the range.

The other thing worth saying is that choosing who should be your fund manager is not simply a hunt for the lowest fund management fee; you also want to be comfortable that the fund manager is going to deliver the best growth for your fund over time.

This can mean a trade-off. It may well be worth paying a slightly higher for someone with a better record of returns over the long term – bearing in mind the old investment manager get out that there is never any guarantee that past performance will be replicated in the future.

When looking at performance be very careful of managers that focus on particularly successful returns in recent years. You want a fund manager that can deliver returns across volatile market cycles – not just in an equity bull market.

You also want to check whether there are other charges connected with the ARF over and above the fund management charge. If you buy your ARF through a broker, for instance, they could be getting commission which will also eat into your fund. And there can be other charges associated with actual trading of investments within your fund.

The bottom line is that there is no way of self-managing your ARF, for instance tapping the industry on an execution-only basis when you want to make a change to your investments or actually draw down funds. You are obliged to use a qualified fund manager and their annual costs will reduce the size of your fund. You need to be happy that you have the lowest possible charges for the best possible investment returns.

That’s a tricky balancing act, one that can never be certain. What is true is that those prepared to do the work in comparing ARF fund managers are more likely to get a better deal.

]]><![CDATA[Budget day looms amid first hints of uncertainty over corporation tax]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/10/04/budget-day-looms-amid-first-hints-of-uncertainty-over-corporation-tax/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/10/04/budget-day-looms-amid-first-hints-of-uncertainty-over-corporation-tax/Sun, 04 Oct 2026 05:00:00 +0000Easily lost in the bumper corporation tax numbers published with Friday’s exchequer returns was the admission by the Government that the State will not collect as much corporation tax this year as it had expected.

The number will be up for sure – hardly surprising given that the headline rate for some of our largest multinationals has risen to 15 per cent from 12.5 per cent – but it will fail to match Government projections.

Back in April, the Department of Finance anticipated corporation tax receipts would come in at €35.3 billion. As recently as last month, it was reported that figures prepared for Taoiseach Micheál Martin and Tánaiste Simon Harris suggested that number would be exceeded by a wide margin.

Now, just weeks later, it has been revised down to €34 billion, fractionally below the fairly conservative estimate in last year’s budget white paper.

Addressing the issue, even as the department unveiled an unexpected €3 billion take from the business tax in September, a spokesman said some payments expected this year would not now arrive until early next year.

Budget Q&A: Submit your questions to our expert panel on budget day

That is very likely but as Harris and his ministerial colleague Jack Chambers put the finishing touches to the budget package for 2027, the first hint of uncertainty about the outlook on corporation tax suggests the time for playing fast and loose with “windfall” corporation tax revenue is coming to an end.

No one should need the Economic and Social Research Institute think tank or the budgetary watchdogs at the Irish Fiscal Advisory Council to realise that using exceptional tax income to fund recurring day-to-day spending is simply irresponsible, especially in a State just one generation on from a catastrophic international bailout.

This time last year, in the budget white paper, the then finance minister Paschal Donohoe saw strong growth in corporate tax underpinning his budgetary arithmetic, alongside income taxes.

Donohoe did add that he expected the tax to top out at some stage. That may be sooner than we think, especially as we are so reliant on a small cohort of companies.

Just three companies, Eli Lilly, Apple and Microsoft, account for close to half of all business tax income. A few years ago during the Covid pandemic, Pfizer would have featured in that sentence. Its subsequent travails illustrate just how fast fortunes can change – and how exposed we might be.

As for income tax, that is certainly delivering on Donohoe’s expectation for now, but even there, the employment outlook is clouded by concerns over geopolitical factors and the impact of artificial intelligence.

The issue that keeps Simon Harris awake at night

Regardless of political party, the focus of every deputy in the Dáil in advance of budget day is on spending, not sound fiscal practice. Politically, expectations have been raised; economically, we are mortgaging the future of our younger generations.

   <description>Pakistan und die Türkei haben am Montag die rasche Verlegung von Soldaten nach Saudi-Arabien beschlossen.    <description>Angesichts der festgefahrenen Situation im Iran-Krieg hat der Chef des weltweit größten Ölkonzerns Saudi Aramco, Armin Nasser, am Montag vor einer bis zu zwei Jahre dauernden Anspannung auf den Märkten für Rohöl und Kraftstoffe gewarnt. <item rdf:about="https://orf.at/stories/3444139/">
   <title>BND-Chef warnt drastisch vor Russland</title>
   <description>Der Präsident des deutschen Bundesnachrichtendiensts (BND), Martin Jäger, sieht die Gefahr einer gewaltsamen Konfrontation Deutschlands mit Russland. Russland führe einen „Schattenkrieg“, warnte Jäger am Montag in einer öffentlichen Anhörung vor dem Parlamentarischen Kontrollgremium des deutschen Bundestags. „Die Konfrontation, in der wir mit Russland stehen, hat eine neue, gefährlichere Qualität: Deutschland ist in Gefahr, in einen gewaltsamen Konflikt mit Russland zu geraten“, so Jäger. Russland dränge Deutschland den Konflikt auf.</description>

What do we know? https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/10/05/reports-claim-trump-tried-to-change-polands-government-what-do-we-know/ Mon, 05 Oct 2026 18:22:20 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=105036

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!

Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.

Media reports claim that US President Donald Trump, during a previously unreported meeting earlier this year with Poland’s defence minister, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, suggested that he leave Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s ruling coalition and form a new government with the right-wing opposition.

Kosiniak-Kamysz has confirmed that the meeting took place, but has not commented on what was discussed. Meanwhile, Tusk himself has said that, while he wants to “maintain discretion”, the information he received from Kosiniak-Kamysz indicates that Trump was interested in discussing the “internal situation in Poland”.

Foreign minister Radosław Sikorski has even more bluntly suggested that the meeting may have served as “an attempt to involve a foreign state in our internal politics”.

Below, we outline how the controversy unfolded, what we know so far, and how senior political figures have commented on the issue.

The context

Poland’s government is a broad coalition that ranges from left to centre right. Although Tusk’s centrist Civic Platform (KO) dominates, it would not have the parliamentary majority necessary to rule if it lost any of its junior coalition partners.

One of those partners is the Polish People’s Party (PSL), which is the most conservative element of the coalition. It has clashed with its partners over issues such as abortion and LGBT+ rights. PSL is led by Kosiniak-Kamysz, who serves as both deputy prime minister and defence minister.

Some elements of the right-wing opposition have suggested that PSL could break with Tusk to form an alternative government, perhaps even with Kosiniak-Kamysz as prime minister. Last year, PSL controversially polled its members on whether they would want to do so. However, PSL and its leader have repeatedly insisted that they remain loyal to Tusk’s coalition.

The Polish People's Party's parliamentary survival is on a knife edge, and could determine whether @donaldtusk's coalition remains in power after next year's elections.@AleksSzczerbiak looks at the challenges facing PSL and how it may respond to them https://t.co/MmswSLNWJE

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 30, 2026

Meanwhile, the government is in constant conflict with President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the opposition. Nawrocki is also a close ally of Trump, who endorsed him during last year’s presidential election.

By contrast, Tusk and his government have clashed with the Trump administration, though they also seek to maintain close relations with the US as Poland’s most important security partner.

The meeting

The news that Kosiniak-Kamysz had met with Trump in March this year came to light in a rather roundabout way.

On 21 September, Poland’s defence ministry announced that a planned meeting at the Pentagon between Kosiniak-Kamysz and his US counterpart, Pete Hegseth, planned for 23 September, had been cancelled “at the urgent request of the American side”.

The official reason for the change of plans was Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to the US at the same time. However, some commentators in Poland claimed that Hegseth had actually cancelled the meeting at the behest of figures close to Nawrocki.

In an effort to debunk those claims, Adam Bielan, a senior PiS figure from the opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party, claimed that he and Nikodem Rachoń, a presidential advisor, had helped to arrange a meeting earlier this year between Kosiniak-Kamysz and a US figure “much more important than Hegseth”.

Rachoń later confirmed this, but said that the meeting had been secret and he was unable to reveal the identity of the US official. He urged Kosiniak-Kamysz to do so.

 

The defence minister obliged, confirming that the meeting had been with Trump himself and had taken place at the White House on 2 March, alongside a ceremony at which a US army officer, Michael Ollis, was posthumously awarded the Medal of Honour for giving his own life to save that of a Polish officer, Karol Cierpica, in Afghanistan.

“I had the opportunity to talk to President Trump for a moment, for which I am very grateful,” said Kosiniak-Kamysz, who noted the role of Nawrocki’s office in arranging the conversation.

What did Trump say to Kosiniak-Kamysz?

Neither Rachoń nor Kosiniak-Kamysz indicated what had been discussed at the meeting. However, last Friday, Dominika Wielowieyska, a leading Polish journalist, claimed that her conversations with various sources, who she did not name, had indicated that Trump used the meeting to encourage Kosiniak-Kamysz to split with Trump and form a new government with the right-wing opposition.

“Trump suggested to Kosiniak-Kamysz that it would be best if he formed a coalition with the right, and that then they would have 100% support from the United States and the presidential administration, and the door would essentially be open to achieving great success for many Poles,” said Wielowieyska, who writes for Gazeta Wyborcza, a leading liberal daily that is hostile towards Nawrocki and sympathetic towards Tusk.

She added that Kosiniak-Kamysz had immediately shared information about the meeting with the government but that Rachoń had failed to submit a note about it to the foreign ministry, despite that being normal practice and despite a request for a note from foreign minister Radosław Sikorski.

Today, Republika, a right-wing broadcaster with close ties to Nawrocki and the opposition, likewise reported, based on unnamed sources, that, “during the conversation with Kosiniak-Kamysz, there were indications that the Americans were interested in a change of prime minister in Poland”.

What has Poland’s government said?

On Friday, Sikorski took to social media to respond to a claim by Bielan that the Trump-Kosiniak-Kamysz meeting was intended to “unblock” negotiations regarding Poland’s desire to host a new permanent US military base.

“In the case of such an important conversation, the organiser [Rachoń] had an obligation to prepare a note,” wrote Sikorski, adding that such a document never reached the foreign ministry. “Could that be because the meeting also served as an attempt to involve a foreign state in our internal politics?”

Z tak ważnej rozmowy organizator miał obowiązek sporządzić notatkę. Do @MSZ_RP ona nie dotarła.
Czyżby dlatego, że spotkanie służyło też próbie zaangażowania obcego państwa w naszą wewnętrzną politykę? https://t.co/0wL0QZBxPv

— Radosław Sikorski 🇵🇱🇪🇺 (@sikorskiradek) October 2, 2026

On Monday, Tusk himself told broadcaster TVN that Kosiniak-Kamysz had informed him about his meeting with Trump immediately after it took place. He added that the subject of the meeting “is too interesting to talk about publicly”, but that military “bases were not the topic of the conversation”.

“The conversation was of a confidential nature, and therefore I feel obliged to maintain discretion. It was more about the internal situation in Poland, that’s how I would put it most delicately,” said Tusk.

Kosiniak-Kamysz himself also confirmed on Monday that the question of a permanent US base in Poland had not been discussed at the meeting. He noted that, in March, that issue was not even seriously on the table, because it was only two months later that Trump announced he intended to send additional troops to Poland

The defence minister did not give any further details about the content of the meeting, which he described as “informal”.

]]> Thousands of protesters trap Polish bishop in church amid anger over dismissal of local priest https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/10/05/thousands-of-protesters-trap-polish-bishop-in-church-amid-anger-over-dismissal-of-local-priest/ Mon, 05 Oct 2026 11:13:32 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=105022

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!

Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.

Thousands of protesters blockaded a bishop inside a church in a Polish village on Sunday – and some even physically attacked him – amid anger over the dismissal of a popular long-serving local Catholic priest.

As a result, police were called in and, after efforts by negotiators to calm the crowd failed, officers escorted the bishop away from the premises after midnight.

„Kościół w Grojcu otoczyło kilka tysięcy osób, parafian i uczęszczających do grojeckiej świątyni. #Aktualnie Okrzyki „jesteśmy z Tobą” dla księdza Józefa Zborka."

Materiał od @FaktyOswiecim pic.twitter.com/3zaqlBCDF6

— Sebastian Kościelnik (@S_Koscielnik) October 4, 2026

The incident took place in the village of Grojec, near the city of Oświęcim in southern Poland. The municipality has an official population of around 3,200, but local media – including the Gazeta Krakowska newspaper and Fakty Oświęcim website – report that around 3,000 people gathered on Sunday evening to protest.

They were angered by the decision to remove local priest Józef Zborek, who has served in the parish for almost 30 years, from his position.

The diocese of Bielsko-Żywiec says the priest was found in church proceedings to have been guilty of “serious and proven irregularities in the performance of his duties”. However, the actual nature of his offences has not been publicly revealed, with the church noting that, under canon law, only Zborek himself can do so.

The case against him was initially reported in 2024. The priest repeatedly appealed against the decision, taking the case to the Vatican. However, the decision to remove him was upheld, with Zborek removed from his position on Saturday.

 

On Sunday, Roman Pindel, the bishop of Bielsko-Żywiec, visited Grojec to meet with the parish council and discuss the situation. Afterwards, he proceeded to the local church to attend the Eucharist.

However, before his arrival, thousands of people had gathered around the church, holding signs saying “Don’t take away our parish priest”. Some burst inside and disrupted the ceremony.

Asked about the reasons for Zborek’s popularity, one woman told Gazeta Krakowska that he had accepted children who had been turned away by other priests for first communion and had “no problem baptising illegitimate children”.

News website Onet reports that one local theory is that the priest was removed from his position because he had not charged parishioners for sacraments. Churches in Poland generally expect people to make payments in return for sacraments such as baptism, confirmation and marriage.

🔴Sceny pod kościołem. Biskup w eskorcie policji. Jest nagranie

Nocna interwencja policji przed kościołem w Grojcu w Małopolsce. Biskup bielsko-żywiecki Roman Pindel wraz z towarzyszącymi mu księżmi został wyprowadzony ze świątyni pod eskortą funkcjonariuszy. Wszystko po… pic.twitter.com/XEXU3LOMXm

— Wirtualna Polska (@wirtualnapolska) October 5, 2026

After the church service had been disrupted, Pindel and several other priests retreated to the sacristy. Social media videos show protesters shouting angrily at the bishop. Some even physically assailed him and had to be pulled away. Once inside, the bishop faced continued verbal aggression.

Shortly afterwards, the police arrived, including specialist negotiators. Pindel spoke to the crowd, explaining that the decision to dismiss Zborek had been confirmed by the Vatican and was final. The bishop reiterated that only Zborek himself was authorised to disclose the reasons for his dismissal.

But, with a large, angry crowd still gathered outside and blocking all exits, the bishop was evacuated under the protection of officers at around 1 a.m.

Hundreds of people have protested in Kraków’s Kazimierz district against plans to evict residents and businesses – including some of the area's famous bars and galleries – from historic church-owned buildings that will be redeveloped into a luxury hotel https://t.co/Xo3SmkWc9g

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 24, 2026

Subsequently, the Bielsko-Żywiec diocese issued a statement saying that the “aggressive crowd” had “threatened the health and lives of the priests”. It also noted that Zborek had been dismissed after a full canon law process in which he had been able to defend himself and appeal.

“We know that many people, especially his parishioners, are experiencing this pain,” they wrote. “However, we ask that you accept this decision in a spirit of faith and in unity with the church.”

]]> Poland updates nuclear strategy with delays to launch of first two plants https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/10/03/poland-updates-nuclear-strategy-with-delays-to-launch-of-first-two-plants/ Sat, 03 Oct 2026 15:00:59 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=104942

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!

The government has updated Poland’s nuclear strategy for the first time in six years, with the new document acknowledging that the country’s first-ever nuclear plant will go online in 2036, three years later than previously planned, and the second in 2040, one year behind schedule.

The delays were widely anticipated, as Poland is already behind the schedule set out in the previous nuclear programme, adopted under the former Law and Justice (PiS) government in 2020.

However, the current administration says the country is still on track for nuclear to become a major part of a more diversified energy mix, providing around 15-16% of electricity generation by 2040.

“This is not just a plan to develop new capacity, but also to build a strong Polish nuclear industry,” energy minister Miłosz Motyka wrote on social media. “We are building a nuclear sector that will drive the Polish economy and serve our security for decades to come.”

Rząd przyjął aktualizację Programu polskiej energetyki jądrowej 🇵🇱

To nie tylko plan rozwoju nowych mocy, ale także budowy silnego polskiego przemysłu jądrowego ⚡️

✅ W sumie do 9 GWe nowych mocy jądrowych;
✅ coraz większy udział polskich firm – docelowo nawet 70 proc. przy… pic.twitter.com/8DorRLUWUj

— Miłosz Motyka (@motykamilosz) September 29, 2026

Under the updated Polish Nuclear Power Programme (PPEJ), Poland plans to develop two nuclear power plants with a combined capacity of around 6 GW to 9 GW, using large-scale Generation III+ reactors.

The first plant, which will have a total capacity of about 3.75 GW, is being built in partnership with an American consortium made up of Westinghouse and Bechtel in the municipality of Choczewo on the Baltic coast. Preparatory work at the site is already underway.

The European Commission last year approved Polish state aid for the project, which is set to receive 60.2 billion zloty (€13.8 billion) in public support between 2025 and 2030

In March 2026, the investor submitted an application to the president of the National Atomic Energy Agency for a permit to construct the plant, with the pouring of the first nuclear concrete scheduled for 2028. The first reactor is now expected to enter commercial operation in 2036, three years later than previously planned.

Construction of Poland’s first nuclear power plant is now set to begin after the @EU_Commission approved Warsaw’s request to allocate 60 billion zloty (€14.2 billion) in state aid for the project https://t.co/Z7BJpRRKnq

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 9, 2025

Plans are already underway for a second nuclear power plant, with construction scheduled to begin in 2032 and the first unit expected to come online around 2040, one year later than previously planned.

Bełchatów and Konin in central Poland remain the preferred locations for that plant, with both areas offering existing energy infrastructure and extensive experience in electricity generation.

Companies from the United States, France and Canada are currently competing to supply the technology and build it, with Poland to choose its partner next year.

 

Alongside expanding nuclear capacity, the programme aims to increase the role of Polish companies in the sector. Domestic firms are expected to account for about 40% of the value of the first reactor project, according to the government.

That share could rise to as much as 70% for subsequent units as Polish companies build up expertise, experience and the necessary certifications.

The government also plans to develop the broader skills base needed to support the nuclear industry, involving universities, research institutes, technical schools and businesses.

A group of prominent Polish businesspeople – including @RBrzoska of @InPostPL and @mati Staniszewski of @ElevenLabs – are investing in a project to develop small modular nuclear reactors being led by Poland's richest man, Michał Sołowow https://t.co/NFoCh9JmYz

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 1, 2026

The expansion of nuclear power is part of a broader effort to reduce Poland’s traditional reliance on coal, which currently generates around half of the country’s electricity. That is by far the highest figure in the EU.

Poland has already been diversifying its energy mix. Coal has declined from supplying 87% of power a decade ago. Meanwhile, the share of renewables has risen from 9% to 29% over the same period.

Under a national energy and climate plan approved in June, Poland aims by 2040 for coal to account for only 0-5% of the energy mix. Around 15-16% will come from nuclear, 7-8% from gas, with most of the rest from renewables: onshore wind (22-27%), offshore wind (18-21%) and solar (14-18%).

Poland’s first offshore wind farm has begun to deliver electricity, with Prime Minister @donaldtusk celebrating the development as a "key element of our energy security and sovereignty".

The government wants 20% of power to come from offshore wind by 2040 https://t.co/EodvInFmrn

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 10, 2026

As well as traditional large-scale nuclear power plants, Poland is also pursuing small modular reactor (SMR) projects.

SMRs, which are prefabricated in factories before being installed onsite, are much smaller than traditional reactors, and proponents say they provide a faster and more cost-effective way of adding nuclear capacity.

]]> Remains of 115 Polish WWII soldiers exhumed in Ukraine https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/10/02/remains-of-115-polish-wwii-soldiers-exhumed-in-ukraine/ Fri, 02 Oct 2026 16:30:58 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=104871

Polish and Ukrainian researchers have exhumed the remains of over 100 Polish soldiers who died in 1939 defending the city of Lviv – which is now in Ukraine but was then part of Poland and known as Lwów – during the invasions by Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union at the start of World War Two.

The work continues recent moves towards reconciliation over the issue of exhuming victims of the war, which has long been a point of contention between the two countries.

ℹ Komunikat o zakończeniu prac ekshumacyjnych na terenie dawnego cmentarza w miejscowości Hołosko Wielkie

⚠️ Zakończyły się prace ekshumacyjne na terenie dawnego cmentarza w miejscowości Hołosko Wielkie, znajdującej się obecnie w granicach administracyjnych Lwowa. Działania… pic.twitter.com/w9rSHuLeua

— Instytut Pamięci Narodowej (@ipngovpl) September 28, 2026

During the work on a 260-square-metre area at Holoskivske Cemetery in Lviv, which began in August, experts found 133 burials. They were identified as 115 soldiers from the Polish army and 18 from the German Wehrmacht.

They died during the Battle of Lwów in September 1939, when Poland sought to defend the city from Nazi Germany, which had invaded from the west on 1 September, and the Soviet Union, which invaded from the east on 17 September.

On 22 September, the Polish forces surrendered and the city came under Soviet control, as Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union had decided when secretly agreeing to divide up Poland in the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact earlier that year.

 

Efforts are now focused on identifying the remains. Experts have taken bone samples for DNA testing, which will be compared with samples from possible relatives.

Another part of the puzzle will be the roughly 2,900 objects – including identification tags, bayonets, helmets and religious items – discovered at the site alongside the remains.

“For us, the identification of the remains is the most important stage of the work, because it is important to return these people their names,” said Dominika Siemińska, a researcher from Poland’s state Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), in a statement published by Lviv city council.

“Currently we have a list of 76 [potential] names,” she added. However, because “so many years have passed, it will be difficult to find their relatives”.

Siemińska also expressed her gratitude to the authorities in Lviv “for providing us with protection, support and the opportunity to work peacefully”. She said that “cooperation with the Ukrainian side is going very well”.

The final stage of the work will be the burial of the recovered remains of Polish soldiers at the Polish cemetery in the Ukrainian city of Mostyska. The date of the ceremony has not yet been announced.

The German remains are being handed over to the Volksbund organisation, which specialises in searching for and reburying German soldiers, said the IPN.

The remains of 55 Poles massacred by Ukrainian nationalists in WWII have been reburied at a ceremony in Ukraine attended by political and religious figures from both countries.

Activists in Poland have launched what they say is the world’s first delivery locker that provides women with abortion pills, access to which is normally tightly restricted.

They have placed the device opposite parliament in Warsaw, a location intended to send a message to the politicians who have made Poland’s abortion laws among the strictest in the world.

The locker (called an “abortomat” in Polish, combining the words aborcja, meaning abortion, and automat, meaning an automatic machine) has been launched by Women Help Women (WHW), a global organisation that provides “self-managed abortion”, and Abortion Dream Team (ADT), a Polish activist group.

They emphasise that the installation “is completely real [and] not an artistic performance”. It consists of 22 numbered lockers and a numeric keypad. Women who have contacted WHM seeking an abortion are given a six-digit PIN code that opens one of the doors, inside which is a package containing the pills.

Recipients can either take the pills at home or do so in a specially prepared space opened last year by ADT and where the locker is located.

 

The activists emphasise that such delivery mechanisms for abortion pills are particularly important in Poland because of the country’s highly restrictive laws.

Abortions are only allowed in two circumstances: if pregnancy is the result of a crime (such as rape or incest) or if it threatens the mother’s life or health. As a result, only 851 legal terminations took place in Poland last year.

However, activist groups such as WHW, ADT and Women on Web (WOW) say that they help tens of thousands of women in Poland obtain abortions each year through other means, in particular by providing pills.

But they face legal risks for doing so: assisting someone in obtaining an unlawful abortion is a crime punishable by up to three years in prison. In 2023, ABW activist Justyna Wydrzyńska was convicted of that offence. Two years later, the sentence was annulled on a technicality and a new trial was ordered.

Żurek, meanwhile, noted that Mielcarek is one of the so-called “neo-judges”, appointed by a judicial body rendered illegitimate by PiS’s reforms. There are legal doubts about the status of such judges and the rulings issued by them, some of which have been overturned on that basis.

In his statement, the justice minister also argued that, under the law, safe passage cannot be issued without a prosecutor’s consent. Lewandowski, however, cited examples of case law that he said disproved this. He also noted that prosecutors had not filed any motion to recuse Mielcarek from the case.

Romanowski served in the justice ministry when it was led by Zbigniew Ziobro, a deputy leader of PiS, who is also wanted by the Polish authorities on suspicion of 26 crimes relating to his time in office.

Like his deputy, Ziobro also obtained asylum in Hungary. When Orbán lost power, Ziobro fled to the United States, reportedly with help from a senior Trump administration official. Poland has requested that Ziobro be extradited, though that process could take years.

Both Ziobro and Romanowski deny committing the crimes they are accused of and claim that they are being pursued as an act of “political revenge” by the government of Prime Minister Donald Tusk.

On a more serious note, the Sejm pointed to the vital role played by dogs in the so-called Speaker’s Guard (Straż Marszałkowska), which is responsible for security in parliament.

“They watch over the safety of all people in the buildings managed by the chancellery of the Sejm,” they wrote, thanking Cobra for eight years of “exemplary” service and wishing her well on her “well-deserved retirement”.

Two weeks ago, the Sejm announced the arrival of a new dog, Otik, who would serve as part of the Speaker’s Guard. He has worked alongside Cobra and another canine colleague, Hela, until now.

Poland’s inflation accelerated to an annual rate of 4.0% in September, up from 3.4% a month earlier, driven primarily by higher fuel prices amid the ongoing conflict in the Middle East and the end of Polish government subsidies that kept down prices at the pump.

The development means that inflation has now risen above the upper bound of 3.5% set by the National Bank of Poland (NBP), which aims to keep the figure at 2.5%, plus or minus one percentage point. Analysts say that an interest rate hike by the NBP is now more likely.

The new preliminary inflation figures from Statistics Poland (GUS), a state agency, show that prices in September were 4% higher than a year earlier, the fastest rise since June 2025. On a monthly basis, prices in September were up 0.7% from August.

The rise was caused in particular by the price of fuel for private transport, which was up 36.1% on a year earlier and 9.2% from the previous month. Energy prices also rose, with electricity, gas and other fuels up 4.9% year-on-year and 0.9% month-on-month.

To shield consumers from the energy crisis triggered by US and Israeli attacks on Iran, Poland has twice introduced temporary measures to curb petrol station prices, including daily price caps and cuts in VAT and excise duty. The system was in place from March to June and again during the the last two weeks of August.

The government has been under pressure from the opposition and opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki to reintroduce the subsidies. However, it argues that Nawrocki’s decision to block a proposed windfall tax on fuel companies makes the measures harder to fund

 

Food and non-alcoholic beverage prices provided some offset, falling 0.5% from a year earlier, although they edged up 0.1% from August. Analysts, however, expect food prices to rise later in the year to reflect lower agricultural yields.

According to GUS’s own estimates, also published on Wednesday, the grain harvest came in 5% lower compared to the last season. This will, in turn, “push the CPI index higher in the coming months”, wrote Erste Bank.

The breach of the upper end of the central bank’s inflation target and the 4% threshold could influence the stance of the NBP’s Monetary Policy Council (RPP), prompting it to hike rates, added Erste Bank analysts.

Zahamowanie spadków cen żywności m/m. Inflacja bazowa prawdopodobnie w dół do 3,0-3,1%r/r, co oznacza że wciąż… pic.twitter.com/AqdIXBthFl

— ING Economics Poland (@ING_EconomicsPL) September 30, 2026

Economists at ING Bank Śląski, meanwhile, expect the first rate hike – after a series of nine cautious cuts between September 2023 and March 2026 – to come in early 2027.

“The RPP may opt to wait, leaving interest rates unchanged in October, with discussions on potential monetary policy tightening beginning in November following the release of the NBP’s new projections,” they wrote on X.

Poland’s benchmark interest rate currently stands at 3.75%, down from a peak of 6.75% reached during the country’s last tightening cycle in 2021-2022, when policymakers were grappling with persistent inflation fuelled by the post-pandemic recovery and the war in Ukraine. Inflation peaked at 18.4% during that period.
