The US ambassador to Poland, Thomas Rose, has launched a planned new Polish-American Centre to be established in Kraków, Poland’s second-largest city. Rose symbolically laid a cornerstone for the new facility and announced a $150,000 (577,000 zloty) grant to restore and preserve the site.

The centre, whose website describes it as a “home for all Polish-American initiatives in Poland”, will be established alongside the famous mound in Kraków created in honour of Tadeusz Kościuszko, a hero of both the Polish and American struggles for independence in the 18th century.

Proud to announce a $150,000 AFCP grant to help restore and preserve the future site of the Kościuszko Mound’s Polish American Center — a living symbol of the friendship between our two nations. Under @POTUS, we remain committed to preserving the shared history that binds the… pic.twitter.com/5atStUIid2

— Ambassador Tom Rose (@USAmbPoland) September 29, 2026

“This is a tremendous opportunity for me, on behalf of President Donald Trump and the American people, to celebrate what I consider the most important relationship the United States has with Europe today,” said Rose at the ceremony on Monday.

“America is fortunate to have many, many good friends around the world. But we have no better friend in Europe,” he added, quoted by broadcaster RMF.

Together with Małgorzata Kidawa-Błońska, the speaker of Poland’s Senate, he laid a cornerstone for the new centre and announced the $150,000 grant, which comes from the Ambassadors’ Fund for Cultural Preservation, a programme run by the US State Department.

“Tadeusz Kościuszko is a symbol of the historical bond between Poland and the USA,” declared Kidawa-Błońska. “There is no better place for the Polish-American Centre than Kraków and the mound commemorating a hero of both nations.”

Tadeusz Kościuszko to symbol historycznej więzi między Polską i USA. Nie ma lepszego miejsca dla Centrum Polsko-Amerykańskiego niż Kraków i kopiec upamiętniający bohatera obu narodów. Niech powołane dziś Centrum dobrze służy naszym relacjom, które budujemy od 250 lat 🇵🇱🇺🇸 pic.twitter.com/8nOkCYDLfD

— Małgorzata Kidawa-Błońska (@M_K_Blonska) September 29, 2026

Kościuszko’s Mound was established in Kraków in 1823, following the pattern of two prehistoric mounds that already existed in the city. It honours Kościuszko, a military officer who had fought against Russian rule over Poland and in the Continental Army during the American Revolutionary War.

Construction of the new Polish-American Centre is being supported by the Kościuszko Mound Committee in Kraków in partnership with USA250PL, the platform for celebrations in Poland of this year’s 250th anniversary of the American Declaration of Independence.

The Kościuszko Mound Committee has long been engaged in efforts to preserve the mound against partial collapses caused by heavy rain. Polish hydraulics manufacturer PONAR Wadowice is also listed as a partner of the new centre.

 

The facility says it “will serve as a living symbol of friendship, understanding, and transatlantic cooperation”, providing “a welcoming space for dialogue, creativity, and exchange”. The centre will house event spaces, conference rooms, and offices.

In June, the centre acted as a patron of a United States–Central and Eastern Europe Connection Weekend at Kraków’s Jagiellonian University. Next year it plans a commemoration of the Battle of Saratoga, where Kościuszko designed fortifications that contributed to the American victory.

Poland has long looked to the United States for support and as an example during its struggle for independence over the last two centuries, including during the period of partitions in the 19th century, the reestablishment of the Polish state after the First World War, and during the later decades of communist rule.

Since the fall of communism, the US has become Warsaw’s most important security partner – including establishing its first permanent military garrison, named Fort Kościuszko, in Poland in 2023.

The US has opened its first military garrison in Poland, and its first anywhere on NATO's eastern flank.

"This is a historic moment," says Poland's defence minister. "We have been striving for years for this word 'permanent' and it has now become fact" https://t.co/knJEcqv4MB

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 21, 2023

Last week, President Donald Trump, in a virtual address to the Polish-American Congress (an entity unrelated to the new centre in Kraków), praised his Polish counterpart Karol Nawrocki, a close Trump ally, and described himself as a “great friend of the people of Poland”.

Shortly before that, Nawrocki had expressed confidence that a planned new US military base in Poland would soon be confirmed, and suggested that it would be named Fort Trump.

City AM https://www.cityam.com/ London's Business Newspaper Mon, 05 Oct 2026 16:53:34 +0000 en-GB hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.0.6 https://www.cityam.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/app_launcher_icon_final_rounded.png?w=32 City AM https://www.cityam.com/ 32 32 213406410 Since SpaceX’s debut, hopes of a blockbuster IPO season have ground to a halt https://www.cityam.com/since-spacexs-debut-hopes-of-a-blockbuster-ipo-season-have-ground-to-a-halt/ Mon, 05 Oct 2026 23:01:00 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2463193

It was hoped SpaceX’s blockbuster June flotation would add rocket boosters to the global IPO  market. But four months on, momentum has come crashing back down to earth.

Wall Street IPOs have slowed considerably since Elon Musk’s $75bn (£56.7bn) listing, damaging what was once expected to be a quarter chock-full of floats.

Smart-ring maker Oura was the latest company to stall its listing just last week, while data centre company SB Energy, petrol station empire EG Group and nuclear energy firm Holtec have all also postponed.

The pauses have cast a dark cloud over the market, particularly for tech megacaps Open AI and Anthropic which were both expected to be hot on Musk’s heels back in the summer.

AI doubts and ‘pop and drop’

Investment bankers and analysts have pinned the shift on lukewarm investor demand coupled with fears over soaring valuations in the booming artificial intelligence sector. 

Renaissance Capital analysts wrote that after the strong second quarter, “issuers prepped deals with price expectations that look too high for today’s choppier market”.

Worries about a downturn in the AI sector have ballooned recently as investors fret over valuations and data centre pushback continues.

SB Energy, which has backing from global tech firm SoftBank, was among the firms attracting backlash over its valuation. It was reportedly targeting $50bn despite failing to bring a single facility online.

Scepticism has also grown in the wake of ‘pop and drop’, where investors initiate aggressive sell-offs in the days following an IPO in response to listings that were vastly oversubscribed.

SpaceX’s shares surged roughly 19 per cent on the first day of trading but have been on a downward trajectory over the past few months, currently hovering around $158.9.

Tech-heavy markets beyond the US have also not been immune to investor doubt. Shanghai listed humanoid robot manufacturer Unitree Robotics surged 460 per cent above its IPO price in its first session, but has since tumbled 46.7 per cent.

Volatility shocks

Renaissance Capital added that “postponed IPOs may cite adverse market conditions, when the reality looks closer to normalised market conditions”.

Firms disconnected to the AI boom were among those who blamed widespread market volatility on their decision to hold off listing.

Oura, which was aiming to raise as much as $2.2bn in a $15.6bn listing , blamed “uncertainty in the IPO market”.

Holtec also cited unfavourable market conditions when it withdrew its IPO filing last month. The growing sense of caution follows months of volatile oil prices sparked by the war in the Middle East and rising bond yields.

Economic uncertainty also led both Open AI and rival Anthropic to hit the brakes on their filings, despite both initially racing to be the first to list.

Anthropic, which is aiming for a jaw-dropping $2 trillion valuation, is now expected to list in mid-November, while Open AI has now pushed back to 2027.

Global uncertainty

While the US has primarily felt the effects of the IPO slowdown, other markets have also suffered.

The UK has recorded just seven listings this year, raising £577m in the first half of the year according to EY. Uzbekistan’s national investment fund Uznif has been coined the only one of note, upon listing a 30 per cent stake in London and Tashkent in May.

“Many companies continue to assess launch timing against a backdrop of fiscal policy developments, monetary policy expectations and wider macroeconomic uncertainty,” said Kat Kravtsov, capital markets director at Pwc UK. 

“While a limited number of listings are expected before the end of 2026, much of the visible pipeline is focused on early 2027. Investors continue to balance long-term optimism with ongoing fiscal, monetary and geopolitical risks.”

London received a shot in the arm last week when African payments firm Airtel Money confirmed its £5.3bn debut for October 14.

But money managers remain broadly pessimistic, as just 32 per cent expect activity to pick up in the next 12 months, according to Berenberg’s latest Investor Barometer. This is down from 63 per cent six months ago.

Fears of IPO derailment have also seeped into Europe, as boutique hotel company Ennismore, which is in a joint venture with French hospitality company Accor has reportedly reconsidered their IPO plans.

Kemi Badenoch has said a “Britannia shield” worth £10bn would fend off missile attacks from hostile countries as the party expanded its defence policy on Tuesday.  Badenoch said the extra spending on defence pledged by the party last month would be allocated on radar, command and interceptor missile systems that would protect Britain’s infrastructure and [...]]]>

Kemi Badenoch has said a “Britannia shield” worth £10bn would fend off missile attacks from hostile countries as the party expanded its defence policy on Tuesday. 

Badenoch said the extra spending on defence pledged by the party last month would be allocated on radar, command and interceptor missile systems that would protect Britain’s infrastructure and military bases. 

The “Britannia shield” would be modelled on Israel’s “Iron dome” that protects the country from Iranian missiles. 

The £10bn investment would take place over a decade, according to party officials. 

The current Defence Investment Plan puts less than £1bn towards a missile system. 

Badenoch said the policy acted as a response to cheap drones taking over battlefields in the Middle East and in Ukraine. 

“The threat is here,” Badenoch said. “Britain must be ready, and Britannia Shield will help make sure we are.”

Defence expansion ‘totally necessary’

An announcement will come in shadow defence secretary James Cartlidge’s speech, in which he will say that a complete interceptor system was “totally necessary”. A Defence Select Committee report last year warned that the UK had “next to nothing” in its missile defence systems. 

The Tories have put pressure on Chancellor John Healey to commit to a substantial uplift in defence spending. The party said last month it would raise defence expenditure to three per cent of GDP by 2030, representing a rise of nearly £11bn a year relative to current spending levels. 

Cuts to housing and child benefits, plus re-routing of investments made by the National Wealth Fund and British Business Bank, would fund extra spending. 

Healey has signalled that he would set out a pathway for defence spending at next year’s Spending Review. 

The Chancellor will also have to find sufficient cash for departmental budgets in order to avoid making sweeping cuts to other areas such as healthcare or justice. 

In June this year, Healey resigned as defence secretary from Sir Keir Starmer’s government over the then-government’s failure to clarify how it would meet Nato targets. 

The Labour veteran accused the Treasury of being “unwilling” to raise military spending to three per cent. Now as Chancellor, he has not yet set out his plans for boosting expenditure. 

]]> 2463089Maurício Alencar Maurício Alencar Top Tory pleads with young people to stay in Britain https://www.cityam.com/top-tory-pleads-with-young-people-to-stay-in-britain/ Mon, 05 Oct 2026 16:51:43 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2463242

Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith has urged young people to stay in Britain and support the Conservatives as he highlighted the Tory pitch to young people amid a row over the party’s commitment to keeping the triple lock pension.  In a speech to party members on Monday, Griffith said Tory policies to scrap stamp duty and [...]]]>

Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith has urged young people to stay in Britain and support the Conservatives as he highlighted the Tory pitch to young people amid a row over the party’s commitment to keeping the triple lock pension. 

In a speech to party members on Monday, Griffith said Tory policies to scrap stamp duty and cut at least one tax at every Budget would help boost young people’s prospects. 

The newly-appointed shadow chancellor said he wanted to reverse a brain drain from Britain that has seen thousands of young people ditch the country to live elsewhere. 

Griffith said: “Many Labour MPs spend their time talking about safe and legal routes for asylum seekers to come here.

“Well, what about safe and legal routes for our own young people to get a job, buy a home, have a good life?  Does that not count?”

He added: “So, if you are thinking of leaving, whether you are young or old, don’t. Many of the things we hold dear are threatened as never before, but none have yet been lost.

“Stay, stay and help us win.”

The effort to win the youth vote looks to shatter a perception that young adults do not vote for the Conservatives. The Office for National Statistics estimated that about 246,000 British nationals left in 2025, with nearly half being aged between 16 and 34.

In the last year, the party has proposed scrapping stamp duty for primary residences, which could slash the cost of buying a home by tens of thousands of pounds, and reforming student loans to stop debt spiralling. 

In his speech, Griffith also announced the Tories would scrap Labour’s mansion tax, which adds a levy on properties worth more than £2m. 

Griffith’s ambition to cut a tax at every budget

The party has committed to keeping the triple lock on the state pension. Andy Burnham said last week that Labour would campaign on a manifesto to reform the uprating mechanism, which ensures that the pension outpaces workers’ wage growth over the long term. 

Griffith told the BBC on Monday Morning that young people were against Burnham’s plan to end the triple lock. The triple lock on pension allows the state pension to rise each year by whichever is highest out of wage growth, inflation or 2.5 per cent.

TalkTalk was founded to take on BT, slash the price of broadband and shake up a market dominated by a handful of incumbents.

But more than two decades later, the challenger has ended up in the arms of the company it was built to challenge.

BT stepped in on Monday to buy Talktalk and its wholesale arm PlatformX Communications out of administration, ending months of increasingly urgent attempts to find a buyer for the debt-laden broadband provider.

The deal keeps 1.5 million retail customers and another one million wholesale connections online, while around 900 employees will move across to BT.

For customers, little changes for now; Broadband remains connected and contracts remain in place. But the deal caps a long decline from one of Britain’s biggest broadband challengers.

Founded by Sir Charles Dunstone in 2003 as part of Carphone Warehouse, Talktalk grew rapidly by undercutting established players. It was spun out as a listed company in 2010 and had around four million customers by 2019.

But cheap broadband becomes a difficult business when customers start disappearing and debts do not.

Talktalk was taken private in 2021 by Dunstone and Toscafund in a deal valuing it at more than £1bn, before spending years trying to get its finances onto firmer ground.

Repeated refinancings bought it time, including a £115m injection led by lender and shareholder Ares Management in February.

But Talktalk remained loss-making despite generating around £1.2bn of revenue over the past year, while its customer base continued to shrink.

By this summer, Octopus Investments entered talks over PlatformX, separate bidders circled the consumer arm and TalkTalk offloaded 120,000 customers to smaller rival Rise Fibre. However, no buyer emerged for the whole business.

A rescue with winners and losers

Allowing Talktalk simply to fail was hardly an attractive option. Its wholesale business supports services across healthcare, emergency services, transport, banking and government, alongside millions of household connections.

BT chief executive Allison Kirkby called the situation “genuinely unprecedented”, while culture secretary Lisa Nandy warned a collapse risked disrupting vital public services.

Talktalk was ultimately sold through a pre-pack administration, allowing BT to acquire the operating businesses immediately and debt-free.

“When we hear the words ‘administration’ or ‘insolvency’, it can sound as though everything stops overnight, but that isn’t necessarily what happens”, Molly Monks, insolvency expert at Parker Walsh, said.

The arrangement is less comfortable for creditors, who are left seeking repayment from Talktalk’s insolvent estate.

BT, meanwhile, gains 1.5 million retail customers and one million wholesale connections.

BT expects the deal to have a roughly £400m cash impact this financial year, although Bloomberg Intelligence’s Matthew Bloxham estimates the implied purchase price itself is below £240m before other costs and working capital.

‘A stich up’

Talktalk was also a major customer of BT-owned Openreach, meaning the deal protects those network volumes while bringing its retail customers under the same roof.

That has inevitably raised competition concerns within the market. Virgin Media branded the takeover a “stitch up masked as a rescue deal”, while Bloxham estimates BT’s fixed-broadband share could rise from around 29 per cent to 35 per cent.

The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) now has until 19 October to examine the deal.

For Talktalk customers, services, prices and contracts remain unchanged for now, with Monks warning against making a “knee-jerk decision” to cancel.

The longer-term fate of the TalkTalk name is less certain, however, with Mayo Wynne Baxter parnter Nick Stockley saying it would not be surprising to see the brand gradually disappear as customers are moved into BT’s wider business.

There would be a certain symmetry to that ending. TalkTalk spent more than two decades trying to loosen BT’s grip on British broadband and in the end, BT was the very company left to rescue it.

Speaking to City AM, associate director at the Institute for Government (IFG), Cassia Rowland, said it is “quite striking that the government is pushing ahead with the plans for judge alone trials in fraud cases, but not in other cases” as it “goes against” recommendations in an independent report published in July by Jonathan Fisher KC, which was presented to parliament.

“It is striking that this goes against the advice of Jonathan Fisher’s independent review. He highlighted that fraud is about dishonesty, and that this should be rooted in the standards of ordinary people and whether someone has behaved in a dishonest way is a citizen judgement,” Rowland said.

“Even though the report recommended to not get rid of juries in complex fraud and related offences, they [the government] are still trying to push ahead with it,” Rowland said.

She added this is an “interesting” move as “there was such a backlash on the idea of these judge only trials for other cases”, and that limiting these jury-free trials to complex cases including fraud, tax evasion, and insider dealing, “is a way of getting some of the benefits without the political difficulty of more general restrictions to jury trials.”

Justice secretary, Alex Norris, told the BBC’s Laura Kuenssberg on Sunday the court backlogs would begin to fall “in this Parliament”, but did not confirm by how much. Norris said it would drop over the next decade “as a result of the changes we’re making”.

Lawyers across the City have also warned against the government’s decision to push ahead with judge-only trials for complex fraud and financial cases.

“The government’s partial retreat on jury trial reform is welcomed, but serious concerns remain if ‘technical and lengthy fraud and financial offences’ will still be heard by a judge alone under amendments to the Courts and Tribunals Bill,” Kingsley Napley partner, Louise Hodges said.

Hodges said: “The risk is that this will introduce more complexity and delays with arguments about what exactly is a ‘technical and lengthy’ fraud and financial offence and how to ensure that this provision will be applied consistently and fairly.”

Sainsbury’s walked away from talks over a merger with smaller rival Morrisons earlier this year, shelving what would have been the biggest shake-up of the UK’s grocery market in decades. 

The UK’s second-largest supermarket chain held preliminary talks with its private-equity-owned rival over a merger of the two firms between November 2025 and February this year, it is understood.

There are no active talks between the two sides but the two parties have not ruled out the possibility of discussions restarting in the future. 

Sainsbury’s attempted to buy discount grocer Asda for £7.3bn in 2019, but had this deal blocked by the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) on the grounds it would reduce competition and push up prices for shoppers.

A deal to combine Sainsbury’s and Morrisons would inevitably draw the scrutiny of the CMA, which could force the firm to sell stores to soothe fears of lessened competition.

Sainsbury’s holds a 15.2 per cent share of the UK’s grocery market, while Morrisons has a 8.4 per cent share, according to Worldpanel by Numerator. 

A combination of the two grocers would take their presence in the market to 23.6 per cent, widening the gap on Asda and Aldi but still below Tesco’s 27.8 per cent. Talks between Sainsbury’s and Morrisons were first reported by Sky News’ Mark Kleinman.

Morrisons creaks under debt pile

Sainsbury’s chief executive Simon Roberts has pushed the supermarket chain to focus on its food sales, which jumped by three per cent to £8bn in the three months to June. 

In July, the group sold Argos to Swift Partners for £120m, after buying the catalogue retailer for £1.4bn a decade ago. 

Morrisons, the UK’s sixth-largest supermarket chain, has been weighed down by a huge debt pile since its takeover by the New-York based Clayton Dubilier & Rice in 2021. 

The group’s net debt grew from £7.1bn to £7.5bn in the year to October 2025 but the grocer last month posted sales growth for the fifteenth consecutive quarter.

Rami Batiéh, who joined Morrisons in 2023, said his turnaround of the grocer is delivering a “broad-based improvement” across the group as he battles to cut costs and keep prices down.

Sainsbury’s operates more than 600 supermarkets and nearly 900 convenience stores. Morrisons runs about 500 supermarkets and more than 1,700 convenience outlets.

Shares in Sainsbury’s fell on news of the collapsed talks, to a loss of about 0.3 per cent at 322p.

Morrisons and Sainsbury’s declined to comment.

Barclays has hiked selected fixed rates on four occasions. HSBC, Lloyds, Nationwide, Natwest, Santander and TSB have all made three rounds of increases.

“Average fixed mortgage rates rising back to three-year highs will be disastrous news for borrowers,” Rachel Springall, finance expert at Moneyfacts, said.

Lenders have hiked their rates as they re-asses how the Bank of England will respond to the developing shocks gripping the economy. One-year ahead inflation expectations increased to 3.3 per cent from 3.1 per cent in August. Longer-term inflation expectations and wage growth predictions also edged higher, according to research, reflecting the heap of price pressures building across the UK economy.

We investigate the mystery of Nigel Farage’s wristwatch. Could the so-called man of the people really wear a £40,000 Patek Philippe Calatrava? Andy Blackmore  starts digging and finds a surprising answer…

Sometimes the watch we wear tells more about us than we would care to admit, far more than any session with a psychologist. With that in mind, I set out to discover the watch that graced Nigel Farage’s wrist in the hope it might give me an insight into what makes him tick.

A quick internet search revealed that I was not the first person to try. There was even a picture, an image of Farage hugging a man in condolence, taken in the wee small hours on 9 May, the night he stood and lost to Craig Mackinlay in Thanet South in the 2015 general election. Sadly, all we can see of the timepiece is a blurred, out-of-focus dial in the bottom left of the frame. So near yet so far.

What is the dress watch on Nigel Farage’s wrist?

The piece in question is a thin, gold-coloured dress watch with a clean, restrained dial, a narrow bezel, and what appears to be a small seconds sub-dial at six o’clock. It has the visual language of a high-end vintage Swiss timepiece.

Someone called Frank Conway had posted the image on Facebook with the question, “Can anyone tell what watch Nigel Farage is wearing here?” A few people had taken the trouble to reply, but one post in particular set my pulse racing. “According to ChatGPT, it’s a Patek Philippe Calatrava.” If this were a Looney Tunes cartoon, you would have seen the barrels rolling behind my eyes and the word “jackpot” written on my eyeballs.

Patek Philippe is the very definition of a “City” watch. The Square Mile summed up in a timepiece. Long lunches and short hair, pinstripes and bowlers, Bow Church, Black cabs, the Bank of England and City police, all distilled and worn on the wrist. It would be a delicious irony were the pint-swilling, salt-of-the-earth populist and anti-establishment everyman wearing the ultimate establishment watch, the very emblem of institutional power and money.

When Roberto Calvi, an Italian financier and head of Banco Ambrosiano, dubbed by the press as “God’s Banker”, was found hanging beneath Blackfriars Bridge on 18 June 1982, he was wearing not one but two Patek Philippes. A wristwatch and a pocket watch by the iconic Swiss maker. The wristwatch had stopped at 1:52 am, which was used to help establish the time of death based on tide levels and water damage.

To the uninitiated, the Patek Philippe Calatrava is a nice watch. I’d go as far as to say it’s a very nice watch. Given its impeccable pedigree, it’s not cheap. The model Farage appears to be wearing, with a yellow gold case and gold dial, retails new for £38,150. With that, I downloaded a copy of the image, cropped and extrapolated it, and asked our AI overlords for their opinion.

Bingo. They both agreed it was indeed a Patek Philippe Calatrava. And as we all know, AI rarely makes mistakes.

Patek Philippe Caltrave: a nice watch

And it chimed with my suspicions: if I had to wager what watch Mr Farage would wear, it would be a Patek. All I needed to do was find a clear image of him wearing it and write my acceptance speech for the British Press Awards. To be honest, after looking at around 18,000 images of Nigel Farage, I deserve an award.

Whether by judgment, image housekeeping, or plain duff luck, it seemed Mr Farage either no longer wore a watch or kept it firmly hidden behind a shirt sleeve. Was our populist PM in waiting worried about pulling a Sarkozy?

A reminder: in the lead-up to the 2012 presidential election, as he navigated the dense throng in Place de la Concorde, Nicolas Sarkozy clasped hands with his enthusiastic supporters. But midway through, without breaking stride, he discreetly slipped off his watch and swiftly tucked it into his pocket. His team later claimed someone was trying to steal it but the press tore into him, interpreting the gesture as both a sign of Sarkozy’s distrust of his own people and a tacit admission that such a lavish timepiece was unbefitting of his position. His friend Jacques Séguéla didn’t help: “If you don’t have a Rolex by the time you reach 50,” he said, “then you have clearly failed in your life.” 

The watch in question wasn’t actually a Rolex – it was a Patek Philippe 5140G-001 Perpetual Calendar in white gold with an opaline white dial, worth about £50,000. The incident torpedoed his campaign with the precision of a French-made Exocet missile.

Not wanting to repeat the mistake, Emmanuel Macron was spotted removing his watch during a live television debate. After catching a glimpse of bling, his hands disappear under the newsroom table, only to emerge mysteriously devoid of ornamentation. On this occasion, the watch in question was a Bell & Ross BR V1-92, which retails for around £1,900 (Macron would later claim he removed the watch because it was banging on the table, which in fairness it was).

It doesn’t end there: Vladimir Putin had an almost identical episode in 2023. The Russian president is known to have amassed an enviable collection of Swiss watches, including an A Lange & Söhne Tourbograph worth some $500,000, a Patek Philippe Perpetual Calendar worth $60,000, and a Blancpain Léman Aqua Lung Grande Date.

Ever the shrewd operator, he would switch these watches ahead of public appearances, instead slipping on a more affordable – and more local – watch by the Imperial Peterhof Factory (IPF); a real man of the people. But a couple of years ago he started a broadcast wearing one of his real watches, surreptitiously slipping it off mid-sentence before clasping his arm as if the strap had merely chafed his wrist. (An interesting aside: Putin is said to have banned anyone from wearing wristwatches during one-on-one meetings with him over potential surveillance and assassination threats.)

Yet try as I might, I could find no record of Mr Farage wearing his flashy watch, just the odd blurred timepiece in a few frames, or him looking at a space on his wrist where a watch should be.

In the end, I was forced to conclude that Mr Farage had stopped wearing a watch – at least in public – around ten years ago. Perhaps the one I spotted on 9 May in Thanet South was an aberration.

Finally we find the watch…

And then… bullseye. I came across a shot of Nigel looking forlornly at the ground at the UKIP party conference, taken on 20 September 2013. While the photographer has focused on his face, the watch is on the same plane. 

As I open Photoshop, I’m literally shaking. The picture is sharp. I can see a name…. It’s a… It’s a bloody Sekonda. A Sekonda, a brand created in 1966 to export watches produced by the USSR’s state factories. It’s about as far from a Patek Calatrava as a watch can get: a budget brand with Soviet origins, now sold in Argos alongside toasters and air fryers. 

I thought I’d better put my findings to the man himself. Is the Sekonda a good watch? And why are there no new photos of him wearing it?

“Not worn one since Covid,” he replied succinctly. So there you go. What a disappointing end to my investigation: Nigel Farage did indeed wear a watch that the average man on the street could afford, that you will almost certainly find on the wrist of at least one punter in your average Wetherspoons. And now he wears no watch at all. Well played, Nigel.

City developers have hailed the Mayor of London’s plans to water down the amount of bike rack space new offices need to provide, arguing that the shift to e-bikes makes these requirements redundant. 

The London Property Alliance (LPA), which represents hundreds of developers in the City and central London, has welcomed proposals to cut down on “large swathes of unused cycle storage space in London’s office buildings”. 

Indoor bike parking is a workplace perk prized by some commuters, but developers are pushing for these spaces to be replaced by other amenities, like gyms and spas. 

The LPA claims that existing requirements for offices to provide space for workers to park their bikes has resulted in huge amounts of unused space. 

More than three quarters (76 per cent) of existing cycle parking space across 21 buildings in the City, Canary Wharf and central London were unused during peak times, research by the LPA has found.

The surplus of space would have been even larger (as high as 84 per cent) if these buildings met the latest bike rack requirements, as set out in the 2021 London Plan.

This calculates bike parking requirements by office space, requiring buildings to provide one long-stay bike space for every 75 sqm. 

Based on the usage observed during the LPA’s research, the industry body says offices need only provide one bike space for every 433 sqm. 

Most of the bike space provided by central London offices is in basements, but the LPA has warned these are among the most expensive and carbon-intensive parts of these buildings to develop. 

Bike racks ‘are wasted space’

Simon Swietochowski, vice chair of the City Property Association, said: “A well-intentioned policy designed to support sustainable travel before the dawn of hire-bikes and dockless e-bikes has inadvertently led to large swathes of unused cycle storage space in London’s office buildings.”

Stuart Lipton, a London-based property developer, told the Financial Times this space can be better used. “You can have a spa, education, cooking experience, games and other things” for work-life balance,” he said.

Developers have pointed towards the surge in popularity of e-bike providers like Lime and Forest as a major reason that workers are no longer bringing their own bikes to the office.

Lime, the UK’s largest e-bike operator, said its number of trips into the Square Mile rose nearly 50 per cent last year. The company’s chief executive, Wayne Ting, has previously called for policymakers and developers to provide more central-London bike parking space.

Responding to criticisms that the firm’s hire cycles are turning London’s streets into an “obstacle course,” Ting said: “We can always do a better job to ensure our bikes don’t block the streets – but we don’t have enough spaces in the city to park our bikes on the street.”

The existing London Plan asks offices to provide bike space based on the assumption that 19 per cent of employees cycle to work. 

A new draft London Plan, drawn up by mayor Sadiq Khan, puts this figure at 10 per cent. This remains below the 6.5 per cent observed by the LPA, but developers say this is a step in the right direction.

Charles Begley, chief executive of the LPA, said: “Moving towards staff-based requirements and allowing more flexible provision should reduce cost and wasted space without weakening facilities for cyclists. 

“We welcome the direction of travel. Getting this right can support cycling while helping unlock the modern workspace London needs for jobs and growth.”

Britain has shed more than half its billionaire wealth in the past two years, fresh research has shown, reviving fears over the scale of the UK’s wealth exodus just days after it emerged that one of the country’s richest men has moved to Monaco.

According to an analysis of the Bloomberg Billionaires Index, super-rich UK residents worth a combined $160bn (£121bn) have either left or loosened ties with UK since 2024 after the Labour government announced a succession of measures clamping down on wealth.

The figure represents more than half of all billionaire wealth in the UK, the analysis said, and comprises the fortunes of a slew of high-profile entrepreneurs including steel tycoon Lakshmi Mittal, Aston Villa co-owner Nassef Sawiris and shipping magnate John Fredriksen.

Since entering office two years ago, ministers have unveiled a string of tax reforms aimed at reducing wealth inequality in the UK and raising revenue. Among the most high-profile changes are the decision to end inheritance tax carve-outs applied to farms and family businesses, the introduction a mansion tax on homes worth more than £2m and ploughing ahead with a pre-election promise to abolish the non-dom regime, a centuries-old carve out allowing wealthy foreigners to pay tax only on income and assets in the UK.

But the changes – combined with persistent speculation over similar crackdowns at future Budgets – have been attributed to driving record numbers of super-rich residents overseas in a pattern that advisers have branded a ‘wealth exodus‘.

Wealth exodus ‘hugely damaging’ for UK

Magda Wierzycka, the founder and chief executive of Sygnia Asset Management, left London for South Africa earlier this year citing the changes to overseas trusts that formed a key plank of the government’s non-dom overhaul. Wierzycka, who is Africa’s richest self-made woman, told City AM that the crackdowns had been “hugely damaging” for confidence in a country that was once a popular bolthole for international moneyed classes.

“The number of people leaving is one thing, but no one is focusing on people who are not coming,” she said. “The entrepreneurs, the wealthy people who previously were drawn to London have taken one look at [the changes] and said, ‘Sorry we’re not coming.’ So that means no investment, no job creation… and this inability to balance the budget.”

Britain’s wealth clamp down comes despite a growing number of countries opting to relax taxes on super-rich foreigners as they seek to lure fresh investment into their economies. In Europe, the likes of Greece, Italy and Portugal have all introduced so-called ‘flat tax regimes’ whereby super-rich immigrants pay a single charge a year for a carve out from all levies on their foreign-held assets.

Earlier this summer, it emerged that feted hedge fund manager Chris Rokos had swapped his UK residency for Greece, having paid an estimated £350m to the Exchequer last year alone. Goldman Sachs’ vice chair Richard Gnodde also left for Milan in the wake of the non-dom tax changes.

Other low-tax jurisdictions like the UAE, Monaco and Switzerland have also proven popular destinations for super-rich Brits moving overseas. According to The Sunday Times, David Reuben has now fully quit the UK having loosened his ties with the country over several years. The publicity-shy property tycoon, who along with his brother Simon are believed to be Britain’s second-richest family, is worth an estimated £28bn and has been among the UK’s richest residents – and biggest taxpayers – for several decades.

“The end of the non-dom regime has left international families facing UK inheritance tax on their worldwide assets, including wealth created overseas, often long before they came to Britain,” said Leslie Macleod-Miller, chief executive of Foreign Investors for Britain. “Add the constant talk of capital gains tax rises, wealth taxes, mansion taxes and exit taxes, and the message is clear: success here is something to be raided, not welcomed.”

The Aston Martin DBX has gained a new derivative, with the GT version focused squarely on enhanced comfort and refinement. 

Although Aston Martin’s luxury SUV was hardly a pared-back vehicle to start with, the DBX GT is designed to showcase the levels of craftsmanship offered by the British marque. 

The new GT acts as a counterpoint to the performance-oriented DBX S in the lineup, with bespoke styling and design details.

Aston Martin CEO Adrian Hallmark said: “DBX GT is aimed at customers who prefer assured elegance over sporting aggression and demand a higher degree of luxury. 

“By refining the visual drama and elevating the interior with new elements of craftsmanship, the DBX GT delivers a true ultra-luxury experience; one which comes with no sacrifice in performance.”

More elegant design for DBX GT

Compared to the visual assertiveness of the DBX S, the GT version of Aston Martin’s SUV looks more subtle and less overtly sporty.

A new double-vaned front grille marks the DBX GT out from other models, with daytime running lights incorporated into its outer elements. Two-piece metal side strakes with contrasting polished and satin finishes are another GT signature.

At the rear, the quad exhaust finishers also make use of polished and satin anodised finishes. The tailpipes are positioned side-by-side, rather than the vertically stacked setup on the DBX S. 

Beneath its bonnet, the GT uses the same 727hp 4.0-litre twin-turbocharged V8 as the DBX S. Performance is also identical, with a 0-60mph time of 3.1 seconds and top speed of 193mph. 

New 22-inch Satin Titanium alloy wheels are fitted, although larger 23-inch items can be selected from the options list.

Interior upgraded, with memory foam seats

On the inside, Aston Martin has redesigned the DBX’s front and rear seats, including a 10mm layer of memory foam to boost comfort. 

Although the GT retains a five-seat layout, the two outer rear seats gain more pronounced headrests and bolsters, aiding lateral support for longer journeys. 

Semi-aniline leather is used extensively throughout the cabin, with no less than 691 metres of thread and 3,297 perforation holes in a single front seat. Each one takes Aston Martin’s craftspeople more than 4.5 hours to create.

Additional sound deadening, along with improved cabin sealing, are also part of the luxury makeover, as are deep-pile carpets. These changes should make it easier to enjoy the premium Bowers & Wilkins audio system, too. 

A panoramic sunroof comes as standard, with anodised metal used for the rotary drive controller and other switches on the centre console.

DBX GT gains its own personality

Along with the design changes, Aston Martin has also tuned the DBX GT’s suspension, recalibrated its automatic transmission and tuned its exhaust note to give the SUV a unique personality. 

Aston Martin’s chief technology officer, Ian Hoban, commented: “The challenge with DBX GT was achieving meaningful improvements in comfort and refinement in everyday use cases, but keeping the same class-leading reserves of performance and handling we have achieved with the DBX S. 

“This was delivered via a combination of small but significant hardware upgrades, together with a targeted suite of calibration changes to the chassis and powertrain. 

“The results are highly satisfying; noticeable reduction in unwanted noise intrusion, greater isolation from road imperfections and a tangible uplift in refinement, but with the breathtaking performance, handling poise and driver connection for which the DBX is renowned.”

Orders for the Aston Martin DBX GT can be placed now, with first deliveries planned before the end of 2026.

Can you bottle that new car smell? Adam Hay-Nicholls goes on a scent tour of the Cotswolds in the new Omoda 7 hybrid electric vehicle

Could you bottle that ‘new car smell’, you’d be on to a winner. That’s the bracing odour of a bold financial decision. That odour is a cocktail of volatile organic compounds: leather, plastic, carpets, seals, coatings and adhesives. A virginal interior untouched by cigarette smoke, damp dogs, BO and takeaway food.

This fresh yet slightly chemical scent has a powerful psychological component. It’s associated with anticipation and reward: collecting your shiny new vehicle, peeling the plastic covers from the seats, seeing the odometer turn over its first miles, knowing that you’re the first and only name in the log book. 

Cars and smells have history together

Cars and smells have history together: there’s a whole subgenre of the auto industry dedicated to creating olfactory delights. The most likely place to find them is in your dad’s Christmas stocking. Car-branded colognes date back to 1988 with the launch of Ferrari Cuvée and Jaguar for Men. Both had an unmistakable whiff of Filofax and red braces about them. Jaguar’s perfume had a brisk green citrus opening that gave way to nutmeg before settling into oakmoss, cedarwood and tobacco. Basically, imagine an XJS sliding into a ditch, hitting a tree and spilling its ashtray. Ferrari’s effort was darker and earthier than the Jaguar pong, with spiciness, balsamic vinegar, leather and musk. 

The trade in car colognes is still going strong today. Ferrari, Jaguar, Bentley, BMW, Aston Martin, Porsche, Mercedes-Benz and Lamborghini all have bottles to sell you. Some are surprisingly well-priced compared to the cost of the four-wheeled product. Ferrari’s Scuderia Black and Bentley’s Azure for Men are priced at £45 and £59 respectively. Lamborghini went the other route, partnering with Xerjoff to create a fragrance that retails for a whopping £331. 

These eaux de toilette are of course designed for the skin, not the dashboard. But we’re living in a brave new world, one in which you can now tailor the way your car smells to better suit your mood. Mercedes, as it so often is, was the first manufacturer to feature a built-in fragrance diffuser. Having previously ushered in anti-lock brakes, the airbag, electronic stability programming (ESP), adaptive cruise control and pre-tightening seatbelts, the latest innovation in the top-of-the-range S-Class is an air conditioning system that can make your car smell better. 

All of which brings us to the Omoda 7, one of the latest Chinese cars to reach our shores and the second after the Merc to have a built-in fragrance bar. The difference is that the Omoda costs three-and-a-half times less than its sweet-scented German rival. The 7 SHS-P (which stands for Super Hybrid System Plug-in) is priced between £32,005 and £35,505 depending on the spec, compared to £112,000 for the Merc. 

It’s a mid-size family SUV – what they call ‘C-segment’ in the biz – and is poised to steal customers from Volkswagen’s Tiguan, which is a little smaller, a little less powerful, and a whole ten grand more expensive. The VW just smells like a new car; there’s no added patchouli or sandalwood. 

My fragrant journey in the Omoda would take me in convoy from SW1 to Devon’s Lympstone Manor, then via Somerset and Wiltshire’s A-roads to Bath and on to the Thyme Hotel in the Cotswolds, before returning to central London 48 hours later. The 450-mile drive would be completed using just two-thirds of a tank of fuel. 

I collected the 7 SHS-P from St James’s Square following a heavy nose session at Floris, where I learned all about smells. This Jermyn Street institution has been a constant since 1730, making it the oldest independent family-run perfumer in the land. It found favour with the aristocracy; Floris let me thumb through weighty ledgers that were nearly a century old, detailing the customer information of George VI and the Queen Mother, the Duke of Windsor and Elizabeth II. I don’t suppose they went in for GDPR back then. Other Floris devotees included Sir Winston Churchill, Cary Grant and Marilyn Monroe. 

After much sniffing and wafting, I settled upon Special No.127, a refreshing citrus blend of bergamot and orange, lavender and geranium, neroli, white patchouli and musk, a combination that could pass as dessert at one of Richard Caring’s establishments. It was created in 1890 for Russia’s Prince Orloff and later found favour with Churchill and Eva Peron. 

Round the corner I get my first chance to really take in the Omoda 7’s exterior. There’s a lot of talk about noses in this piece, and the Omoda’s is notable in that there’s very little going on. Its broad, borderless grille dissolves into the bumper like an oversized version of the ‘egg crate’ grille first seen on the Ferrari Roma, which has become a design trend du jour. It leaves a clean and EV-like expanse between the Omoda’s razor-thin headlights. There’s no great chrome moustache or badge to shout about; instead the nose has a blank, futuristic expression that brings to mind high-end consumer electronics.

Inside, things are equally minimalistic. There’s very little to interrupt the slab of touchscreen in the middle of the dash. It looks smart and contemporary and controls pretty much everything in the vehicle, which is far too forward looking to bother with such anachronistic flourishes as physical switches.

My four-hour expedition down the M3 and A303 is comfortable and relaxing, and I feel as charged as my steed’s battery as I pull into Lympstone Manor, which sits on the River Exe between Exeter and Exmouth. This isn’t just a lovely hotel, it’s also the restaurant of chef-patron Michael Caines (not the one who ordered the doors to be blown off, the other one). 

Following an evening of nine courses, including a ballotine of duck liver with Sauternes jelly, and a thumpingly delicious roast pigeon with celeriac and truffle purée (complex aromas indeed), it was back on the road with the thrifty Omoda, which had barely sipped its decanter of Chateau Unleaded. I didn’t dare distract myself with the fragrance bar on the way down, but at standstill I gave the olfactory options a good prod. 

How does the Omoda 7 smell?

First up ‘Charming Air’, with its delicate top notes of orange, citrus and green leaf, middle notes of rose, peony and geranium, and base notes of amber, musk, cedar and cashmere. Not all that different from the Xerjoff x Lamborghini spray, come to think of it. The Omoda 7 only costs 100 times more than a bottle of Lambo’s fragrance and it comes with five seats and a 201bhp hybrid powertrain, which is a bargain, when you put it like that. Zero to 62mph takes it 8.4 seconds; not quite Urus speeds, granted, but at least you can enjoy the smell for those extra few seconds.

My fellow travellers and I swung by the ivy-covered Bath Priory for lunch, before I cued up the next in-car perfume and our convoy headed for the Cotswolds. ‘Forest Bath’ has nothing to do with the Georgian city’s surrounding woodland and everything to do with the Omoda’s scent option of green leaf, eucalyptus and amber. Arriving at the restaurant Thyme, somewhere close to the village of Fyfield, we’re led through a gorgeous, pungent herb garden before taking over the kitchen for a cookery lesson. I knocked up a very serviceable tapenade under the direction of resident teacher and MasterChef champion Marjorie Lang. I do enjoy a road trip where you go home with jars of stuff. 

The final day’s stretch took us back to London, where I sampled the last of the Omoda fragrances. ‘Dark Temptation’ is a pleasing and not at all slutty or psychotic blend of green leaf and coriander, black rose and saffron, musk, ebony and patchouli.

I soaked it in until we arrived at our last    perfumer, one from the newer end of the scene than Floris. Perfumer H is located in Marylebone; a mid-century modern boutique that creates beautiful and unconventional fragrances. They waft them at me and I nod appreciatively, despite the fact my nose has been used so much over the last few days it’s threatening to go on strike. 

As they regale me with anecdotes about fragrances, I mull over my time with the Omoda 7. It’s impressively priced and even cheaper to run. It’ll do around 40 real-world miles-per-gallon, which has never been more important thanks to Donald Trump’s misadventures in the Middle East. If you’re sticking to urban areas you can squeeze 55 silent and emission-free electric miles out of it, but having a plug-in hybrid over a full EV means it’s much more flexible for when you just need to get in and drive. 

On my driveway right now I have the all-electric Lexus ES 350e, which costs double what the Omoda does and, I discovered last weekend, only has a 273 mile range, rather than the 361 miles the manufacturer claims. It just so happened I had to drive it 271 miles to a rural area with no time to dick around with chargers. I’m still having anxiety dreams. The Omoda 7 will do 770 miles on a tank and charge (confirmed, not make-believe), and it only takes five minutes to get back on the road when you’re running low on juice. 

It’s also lighter than its EV competition, so it handles seamlessly for a car of this class apart from a slight numbness of the steering, which is typical in this day and age. The build quality, materials and equipment compare well to its Japanese, Korean and German rivals, and knocks the Stellantis brands into a cocked hat. 

I returned from my road trip smelling like a high-class boudoir, and with a shockingly small bill for petrol even with the Hormuz-inflated prices. While some of the scent follows me as I exit the vehicle, there’s nothing overpowering about the Omoda 7. It’s subtle, delicate, something you can imagine becoming a staple – but it will never lose that new car smell.

Aldi chief executive Giles Hurley has claimed that bigger supermarkets try to entice shoppers with loyalty discounts that “isn’t supportive, isn’t transparent, and doesn’t help customers plan and budget”.

Responding to Hurley’s comments, Lidl chief executive Ryan McDonnell told reporters: “Listening to our customers and investing to improve the retail experience is what we’re about. Lidl Plus is something that’s resonating fantastically well with customers, and we see that in switching data as well.”

Lidl, the UK’s fifth-largest supermarket chain, grew its revenue by 10.8 per cent to £13bn in the year to February. The group’s operating profit jumped by 10 per cent to £345m. Its statutory pre-tax profit increased by a third to £206m, owing to lower interest costs.

Lidl said it saw 43m more visits year on year, attributing more than £650m in sales to shoppers switching from its competitors. 

The grocer said this higher footfall helped it sell 486m more products in this year than the one before, adding that it saw “significant growth” across meat, poultry, fruit and vegetables.

Lidl invested £315m in price-cuts and promotions, it said. British supermarkets have ramped up attempts to slash prices in recent months, as they compete for shoppers who feel increasingly cash-strapped as a result of the Iran war.

Lidl and Aldi step up expansion

Lidl operates more than 1,000 stores in the UK and opened 40 new sites in the year to February. Alongside new locations, the group invested £43m in upgrading 70 existing shops.

The company’s store upgrades are focussing on more self-checkouts, energy-efficient lighting and freezer upgrades. Some supermarkets saw their freezers struggle with record heat over the summer.  

In April, Lidl announced that it will open more than 50 new supermarkets in the year to February 2027, as part of a £600m investment in widening its reach. 

The UK’s competition watchdog, the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA), has provisionally decided that Lidl and Aldi will have to comply with the same land rules as their competitors.

The German discounters had been exempted from rules preventing grocers from restricting rivals from opening stores nearby, but this loophole is set to end.

But the two grocery chains have said the new rules will not slow their expansion plans. Last week, Aldi announced a £900m investment in opening 40 new stores next year.

Lidl’s McDonnell said on Monday: “As a discounter, we embrace fair market competition and this outcome will now slow our momentum as we continue expanding the store network.”

Lidl is owned by the Schwarz Group, which is weighing up a deal to take over dozens of Tesco stores in eastern Europe.

Tesco, the UK’s biggest supermarket, is planning to offload its entire European division outside of the UK and Ireland, which includes hundreds of locations in Hungary, the Czech Republic and Slovakia.

Broadband giant BT has agreed to snap up embattled telecommunications firm Talktalk in a move that has prompted the government to weigh in.

The FTSE 100 group said on Monday it had acquired Talktalk and its wholesale arm PlatformX Communications (PXC) out of administration on a debt-free basis.

The deal, for an undisclosed sum, is estimated to take a £400m bite out of BT’s bottom line, from transaction fees, working capital, a £60m trading loss, and £100m in uncollected Openreach revenues.

It will provide “immediate reassurance” for Talktalk employees and its 1.5m retail customers and 1m wholesale users across the UK, BT said.

Culture secretary Lisa Nandy said: “Phone and broadband services are vital national infrastructure. If TalkTalk services fail, there is a genuine risk to life and public services – including to hospitals, schools and emergency care.

“These are unprecedented circumstances that require action now. That is why I am acting with urgency to ensure that impacts on public health, critical national infrastructure and supply to vulnerable customers are fully considered as part of this process.”

The government said it was acting under Enterprise ‌Act powers that will permit Nandy to consider the wider public interest once the ​Competition and ​Markets Authority (CMA) has reported on competition concerns. The CMA has been directed to report back by 19 October.

Ares Management, the US private credit giant which has lent Talktalk millions of pounds, has warned officials that at BT deal would undermine the UK’s pro-business credentials and damage Britain’s standing as a destination for international investment.

‘Genuinely unprecedented’

Talktalk, which is the UK’s fourth-largest broadband company, was founded in 2003 by Charles Dunstone as part of the Carphone Warehouse group. It has suffered under a highly competitive telecoms market and saw its customer numbers shrink from highs of 4m in 2019.

The group has debts reported to be around £1.4bn and has required repeated injections of additonal funding. This March, Talktalk announced £115m of new facilities from its existing shareholders and lenders, which was made up of £65m of term funding and a £50m working-capital facility.

In the last 12 months, TalkTalk made around £1.2bn in revenue and was loss-making. It is estimated to employ around 900 people.

Allison Kirkby, chief executive of BT, said: “This is a genuinely unprecedented situation, where millions of citizens and businesses were at risk if Talktalk had collapsed. BT is the digital backbone of the country, with a presence in every postcode.

“We have been connecting the nation for generations, stepping up in the moments that matter, and BT acquiring Talktalk is now the only viable option to keep millions of customers connected and supported.”

Kirby added the “immediate priority” was to stabilise the business and provide a “safety net” for those who rely on Talktalk.
